theory_units.title: Maintaining Direction with Static Anchor & Contrasting Motion (Same Half-Screen)
theory_units.summary: A static foreground element (person or object) positioned in one half of the screen can anchor the audience's orientation, allowing a moving subject to change its screen direction within the other half of the screen without losing a sense of continuous movement.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to show a subject moving in contrasting directions across cuts (e.g., right-to-center then center-to-right) while preserving a continuous sense of direction for the audience, often with a change in camera angle.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience maintains a continuous sense of the moving subject's direction despite opposing screen movements, due to the consistent static anchor.
theory_units.caution: The static and moving subjects must be positioned in the same screen area across both takes.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Direction with Static Anchor & Contrasting Motion (Pause)
theory_units.summary: When a continuous movement includes a pause, contrasting screen directions in the same half-screen, anchored by a static element, can be used around the pause to maintain a clear sense of the subject's overall direction.
theory_units.applies_when: For movements that include a pause, where maintaining a continuous sense of direction is crucial, even with opposing screen movements.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience perceives the movement as continuous relative to the static anchor, despite the pause and opposing screen directions.
theory_units.caution: The principle relies on the moving subject's consistent relationship to the static anchor in the same screen sector.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Direction with Static Anchor & Contrasting Motion (Moving Camera)
theory_units.summary: The principle of maintaining audience orientation with contrasting movements in the same screen sector (via a static anchor) can be effectively applied even when one of the camera placements involves a moving camera (e.g., a tracking shot).
theory_units.applies_when: When incorporating tracking shots into a sequence where opposing movements occur, but a continuous sense of direction must be maintained for the subject.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience perceives continuous motion and direction for the subject, even with a moving camera and opposed screen movements in the same screen half.
theory_units.caution: The opposed movements must occur on the same side of the screen in both shots, relative to the anchor.

theory_units.title: Cut Continuity Elements
theory_units.summary: To ensure a smooth visual flow and prevent audience confusion, cuts between shots must match key elements like position, movement, and eyeline.
theory_units.applies_when: Anytime two strips of film recording segments of the same continuous movement are joined.
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamless and unconfused presentation of material, maintaining audience immersion and understanding of spatial and temporal relationships.

theory_units.title: Cutting on Movement for Smooth Transitions
theory_units.summary: Cutting during or immediately after a subject's movement (even subtle ones) distracts the audience from the visual 'jar' or change in volume that occurs when transitioning between shots, making the cut seamless.
theory_units.applies_when: Almost every cut between two shots, especially when there is a change in camera distance or placement relative to the subject.
theory_units.expected_effect: Eliminates visual jumps, making cuts unnoticed by the audience and maintaining narrative flow and immersion.
theory_units.caution: Cutting between two static shots where no movement occurs will result in a jerky, noticeable transition.

theory_units.title: Cutting After the Movement (Continuity)
theory_units.summary: An editing technique where the cut to a closer shot occurs a few frames *after* a subject's or camera's movement in the preceding shot has fully completed, often on the same visual axis.
theory_units.applies_when: When approaching on the same visual axis; when a player performs vertical or neutral (towards/away) motion; when the camera travels or pans and stops; when an unemphatic visual approach is desired; to fulfill the audience's unconscious desire for a closer look at a subject.
theory_units.expected_effect: Smooth transition, advances the view, draws audience attention to the subject, provides a closer look, unemphatic visual approach, avoids unpleasant jumps if image size change is great and subjects don't move substantially.
theory_units.caution: Movements across the screen are generally less ideal for this type of cut; seldom used for cutting back from close to full shot (primarily for forward cuts); more dynamic approaches are typically used for receding movements or movements across the screen.

theory_units.title: Cutting on the Movement (General Principle)
theory_units.summary: A technique for continuity cuts that involves joining fragments of a continuous action from separate shots to create vitality and smoothly change viewpoint.
theory_units.applies_when: When changing viewpoint smoothly around one or a group of characters; to create vitality peculiar to the film medium; when performing continuity cuts of a single action across multiple shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhanced vitality, smooth change of viewpoint, seamless transition between shots of a continuous action.
theory_units.caution: The 1/3-2/3 rule is a good starting point, not a strict rule; all rules can be broken if understood. Ensure matched speed of movement between shots during shooting. If movement speeds are ill-matched, it is generally more satisfactory for the movement to appear faster in the second fragment.

theory_units.title: Covering Turning Movement
theory_units.summary: Strategies for photographing and editing a character's turning motion to maintain continuity and provide appropriate coverage.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character performs a turning motion on the spot (e.g., 90°, 180°, or full circle).
theory_units.expected_effect: Smooth capture of the turning motion, maintaining consistent character screen positions (if desired), and providing appropriate visual information to the audience.
theory_units.caution: Internal reverse angles and parallel camera positions are unsuitable for shooting continuous turning motion due to divergent coverage. Full circle turns are generally the least interesting of the three options for an action cut.

theory_units.title: Dividing Turning Movement into Two Shots
theory_units.summary: Divide a single turning movement into two shots using reverse angle camera coverage, ensuring players maintain their relative screen areas.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a single player's turning movement, aiming for a matched action cut while emphasizing the turn and maintaining spatial coherence.
theory_units.expected_effect: A smooth and continuous transition across a turning action, making the movement clear to the audience despite the cut.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Visual Axis and Screen Sector for Turns
theory_units.summary: When cutting between two shots of a turning movement, maintain the same visual axis and position the player in the same sector of the screen (center or one of the three side areas).
theory_units.applies_when: Editing together multiple shots of a character's turning motion to ensure spatial continuity and clarity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhanced spatial continuity and audience orientation, making the turn feel seamless and understandable.
theory_units.caution: Failing to maintain consistency can lead to confusing or disorienting cuts.

theory_units.title: Expanding/Contracting Group with Matched Turn
theory_units.summary: Widen or narrow the group of players introduced in the second shot, using a dominant player's turning motion as a natural trigger to introduce or exclude other characters.
theory_units.applies_when: Introducing or removing characters from focus within a scene by linking their appearance/disappearance to a character's turning movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Subtly directs audience attention to the dominant player while dynamically altering the group composition, emphasizing or de-emphasizing supporting characters.

theory_units.title: Right Angle Turn for Group Introduction/Exclusion
theory_units.summary: When a dominant player turns 90 degrees, cut to a right-angle camera site. Position the dominant player (center or side) to dictate how newly introduced performers occupy the remaining screen area.
theory_units.applies_when: Introducing new characters or shifting focus within a group during a character's 90-degree turn, often as part of a group widening/narrowing strategy.
theory_units.expected_effect: Subtly integrates new characters into the scene's composition, using the turning motion as a natural transition point, and controlling their prominence.

theory_units.title: Group Widening/Narrowing with Common Visual Axis Turn
theory_units.summary: Employ an advance on a common visual axis to widen or narrow a group during a dominant player's turning motion, using the turn as justification to introduce or exclude other players.
theory_units.applies_when: When using a turning motion to naturally expand or contract the visible group of characters for compositional or narrative reasons, maintaining a smooth visual flow.
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamlessly adjusts group size on screen, directing focus based on the turning character's action, while preserving spatial continuity.

theory_units.title: Using Reverse Angles for Group Composition Changes
theory_units.summary: Combine external and internal reverse angles around a turning player to widen or reduce the group presented on screen, thereby shifting visual emphasis to the central performer.
theory_units.applies_when: Adjusting the number of visible characters in a scene, particularly when a central performer is turning, to emphasize them or alter group dynamics.
theory_units.expected_effect: Changes the perceived size of a group, drawing focus to or away from the central turning character, making them visually dominant.

theory_units.title: Prioritizing Foreground Motion Match
theory_units.summary: In shots involving both foreground and background movement, the foreground motion is dominant and must be precisely matched across cuts to ensure continuity.
theory_units.applies_when: Editing shots with complex movements, especially when characters are on moving vehicles or against dynamic backgrounds.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures smooth and believable continuity for the primary action, preventing jarring cuts that distract from the main subject.
theory_units.caution: Failure to precisely match foreground motion can lead to confusing or jarring edits that break immersion.

theory_units.title: Opposed Direction Turn with External Reverse Angles
theory_units.summary: Cover a lone performer's 180-degree turn using a pair of external reverse angles at the extreme points of the arc, resulting in opposed senses of screen direction for the movement.
theory_units.applies_when: Emphasizing a full 180-degree turn of a lone performer, especially for sudden turns, while maintaining dynamic visual interest.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dynamic visual effect of opposed motion that, despite the direction change, remains clear to the audience because the performer's action is understood (e.g., starts and concludes facing us).
theory_units.caution: While effective for clear turns, unclear framing or an ambiguous turn might confuse the audience.

theory_units.title: Two-Person Turn with External Reverse Angles
theory_units.summary: When two players turn simultaneously, using external reverse angle camera sites will cause them to switch screen positions between shots, applying the same principle as for a lone performer's opposed direction turn.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering a simultaneous turn of two characters, maintaining dynamism while clearly showing their individual turns and interactions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Dynamic screen movement as characters switch positions, maintaining clarity of their combined action despite opposed screen directions.

theory_units.title: Emphasizing Arc-Shaped Turns While Walking
theory_units.summary: To stress a change of direction when an actor turns as he walks (an arc-shaped movement), use a pair of reverse external sites or a right angle camera position.
theory_units.applies_when: Highlighting a significant or dramatic change in direction during a character's walking turn.
theory_units.expected_effect: Amplifies the visual impact of the turn, making the change of direction more pronounced and noticeable to the audience.

theory_units.title: Editing Opposed Direction 180-degree Turn
theory_units.summary: When covering a 180-degree turn with external reverse angles, use the first half of the turn from the first shot and the complementary second half from the second shot. In the first, the player moves from center to one side; in the second, from the opposite side to the center.
theory_units.applies_when: Executing a dynamic cut on a 180-degree turn, particularly a sudden one, using reverse angles.
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamlessly connects two shots of opposed movement, maintaining clarity of the overall turn because the performer's full movement is clear.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the cuts are precise at the midpoint of the turn for optimal smoothness and to avoid jarring discontinuity.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Screen Sector for Divided Turns
theory_units.summary: When dividing a turning movement into two shots, the performer must be located in the same screen sector in both shots (e.g., center, left third, right third) to maintain continuity.
theory_units.applies_when: Editing any turning movement that is split across two cuts, regardless of camera angle choice.
theory_units.expected_effect: A seamless and non-disorienting transition, as the audience can easily track the performer's consistent position on screen.
theory_units.caution: Failing to maintain the same screen sector can lead to disorienting jump cuts or confusing spatial relationships.

theory_units.title: Framing Rising Movement within Screen Boundaries
theory_units.summary: To keep a rising movement within the boundaries of the screen frame and manage emphasis, cut from a medium shot to a backward full shot (for context) or to a forward close shot (for intensity).
theory_units.applies_when: Covering a character's rising motion while ensuring they remain visibly within the frame and controlling the audience's focus.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains visual continuity of the rising action, either expanding the view to show context or intensifying focus on the character's reaction/effort.

theory_units.title: Rising Movement with Right Angle Camera
theory_units.summary: Cover a rising movement using a right angle camera position to distinctly register the upward motion of the player.
theory_units.applies_when: When desiring a dynamic or alternative perspective on a character's rising action, emphasizing the verticality of the movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a clear visual of the vertical motion from a side perspective, adding dynamic variety and potentially revealing elements within the scene.

theory_units.title: Rising Movement with External/Internal Reverse Angles for Number Contrast
theory_units.summary: Use a combination of an external and an internal reverse angle to cover a rising motion, which provides 'number contrast' in the picture area.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a rising motion and simultaneously wishing to alter the perceived number of characters or elements in the frame, or to create a dynamic visual shift.
theory_units.expected_effect: Dynamically shifts the composition around the rising performer, potentially altering visual emphasis or context through a perceived change in the number of visible elements.
theory_units.caution: The exact nature of 'number contrast' should be clearly defined by the director's intention for the scene.

theory_units.title: Sitting Movement with Common Visual Axis
theory_units.summary: When covering a sitting motion with camera sites on a common visual axis, keep the player in the same screen sector in both shots. Shot sizes can vary (e.g., full to medium or vice versa) to adjust emphasis.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering a character sitting down in a way that emphasizes smooth, continuous motion and spatial stability, without disorienting the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamless transition of the sitting action, maintaining character position on screen and avoiding disorientation while allowing for varied shot emphasis.

theory_units.title: Sitting Movement with External Reverse Angles for Opposed Arcs
theory_units.summary: Cover a lone performer sitting down using external reverse angles, which will register as two opposed arc movements on the screen. The opposed directions are obtained due to the player having a profiled body position in both shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Emphasizing the arc-shaped nature and physical effort of a character sitting down, or creating a more dynamic cut while maintaining clarity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Dynamic visual representation of the sitting movement through contrasting screen directions, while remaining clear due to the recognizable body action and profiled position.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the profiled body position is clear in both shots to avoid confusion despite the opposed screen directions.

theory_units.title: Opposed Screen Motion via Internal/External Reverse Angles
theory_units.summary: Cutting between internal and external reverse camera positions for a continuous movement can create a perceived opposition in screen direction and character orientation, even for a single moving player.
theory_units.applies_when: When a single character performs a continuous action (e.g., reclining) and the director wants to visually emphasize the transition, create a dynamic sense of opposed screen direction, or shift the audience's perspective on the character's orientation (e.g., front to back).
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience perceives a visually dynamic continuous movement with a strong sense of directional change and a shift in perspective on the character (e.g., from seeing their front to their back), enhancing engagement with the action.

theory_units.title: Dramatic Angle Shift with Reverse Sequence Opposed Motion
theory_units.summary: Reversing the internal/external sequence (cutting from an external rear view to an internal front view) for a continuous action can achieve contrasting movement directions and allow for the introduction of dramatic camera angles, such as a low angle to emphasize a fall.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting a continuous action, particularly one with impact like a fall, and wanting to show contrasting movement directions while dramatically shifting the camera's perspective (e.g., to emphasize vulnerability or impact with a low angle).
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience perceives contrasting movement directions within the same screen sector, and the specific change in camera angle (e.g., a low angle) enhances the dramatic impact or highlights a particular detail of the action.

theory_units.title: Fragmenting Unified Two-Player Movement for Opposed Directions
theory_units.summary: When two players move together as a single unit, their continuous movement can be fragmented across two external reverse shots to create an effect of opposed screen directions for both characters, while maintaining their relative screen positions and screen areas.
theory_units.applies_when: When two characters are moving in unison (e.g., reclining simultaneously) and the director wants to dynamically complete their movement with visual directional contrast, without disrupting their unified action or spatial relationship on screen.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience perceives a continuous, unified movement of both characters, but the transition between shots dynamically reverses their screen direction, adding visual interest while preserving their coherent spatial relationship.
theory_units.caution: Ensure characters maintain constant screen areas from shot to shot to preserve the sense of unity and continuity.

theory_units.title: Opposed Directions & Screen Area Exchange for Single Actor Movement
theory_units.summary: To create opposed senses of movement direction and an exchange of screen areas for a single performer's continuous motion, film the actor moving from side to center in a first shot (e.g., full shot, back to camera) and then from the opposite side to center in a reverse external shot (e.g., close shot, facing camera), ensuring the main actor remains centrally framed.
theory_units.applies_when: When a performer's continuous movement needs to be shown across two shots where perceived screen direction is reversed, and the performer's screen centrality is maintained, causing other background elements or partners to dynamically shift screen areas.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience experiences a dynamic shift in screen direction and the positioning of background elements/partners, while the main performer remains consistently anchored in the center, making the continuous motion visually engaging and controlled.
theory_units.caution: It is crucial that the primary performer is consistently kept in the center of the screen; supporting elements or partners will naturally shift sides to accommodate the reverse.

theory_units.title: Basic Linear Movement Coverage (Away & Towards Camera)
theory_units.summary: Use external reverse camera coverage to film linear walking or running movement in neutral directions (away from, then towards the camera) to show a player's continuous trajectory. Crucially, all camera positions must be on the same side of the line of movement to ensure background continuity.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming a character walking or running in a generally straight line and needing to show both their departure and subsequent approach to a point, maintaining clear spatial continuity and orientation.
theory_units.expected_effect: A clear, spatially coherent, and continuous portrayal of linear movement, with a strong sense of consistent environment due to stable background elements.
theory_units.caution: Both camera positions must be on the same side of the line of movement. Any identifiable background object seen in the first shot must appear in the same screen sector in the second shot to avoid audience disorientation.

theory_units.title: Reversed Linear Movement Coverage (Towards & Away Camera)
theory_units.summary: A variant of basic linear movement coverage where the player first approaches the camera in a frontal shot and then moves away in a rear shot, without exiting the screen in either shot, maintaining a neutral spatial direction.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character's linear movement needs to be shown from an initial approaching perspective, followed by a receding perspective, with the intent to keep the character within the frame throughout their movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience sees the full range of the character's linear movement, emphasizing both their approach and departure without losing them from the frame, maintaining a neutral and direct spatial journey.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the player does not exit the screen in either shot to maintain continuous presence.

theory_units.title: Two-Shot Discontinuous Walking Movement
theory_units.summary: To cover a walking movement that is intentionally interrupted (where a player approaches, stops, then goes away), use two distinct shots: one capturing the approach and stop, and a reverse shot for the departure towards a new goal.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character's linear movement includes a significant pause, a moment of contemplation, or an interaction before they continue their journey in a new direction or towards a different objective.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly communicates the pause in action, highlights the character's immediate focus (e.g., looking off-screen), and defines their subsequent commitment to a new direction, effectively breaking and re-establishing the continuous flow.

theory_units.title: Four-Shot Discontinuous Movement to Goal Strategy
theory_units.summary: To cover an extended, discontinuous movement where a player approaches an identifiable goal (another player), use a four-shot sequence involving alternating external reverse camera positions. This strategy segments the journey and arrival, maintaining actor screen sectors throughout.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting a significant, extended, and discontinuous movement towards a specific person or object, where the progression of the journey, anticipation, and the final arrival/interaction are important to emphasize.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a detailed and progressive narrative of the character's movement, clearly defining stages of departure, anticipation, and final interaction with the goal, while maintaining strong spatial continuity.
theory_units.caution: Both actors must maintain constant screen sectors across all shots in the sequence to ensure smooth spatial continuity and avoid disorientation.

theory_units.title: High Angle Reverse Shots for Perceived Vertical Movement
theory_units.summary: Filming a neutral horizontal walking or running movement from two high camera positions set on reverse angles will make the player appear to ascend in one shot and descend in the other, while surrounding objects dynamically shift screen sides.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director wants to introduce a dynamic vertical illusion to an otherwise horizontal movement, or to emphasize the shifting environment and changes in perspective around the moving character.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a unique and engaging visual dynamic where horizontal movement gains a perceived vertical dimension (ascending/descending), making the scene more visually interesting and potentially surreal or disorienting, and highlights the changing environment.
theory_units.caution: The pronounced shifting of objects or persons around the performer from one side of the screen to the other might be disorienting or distracting if not intentionally integrated into the scene's narrative or mood.

theory_units.title: Altering Real Movement for Perceived Screen Continuity (Diagonal)
theory_units.summary: To maintain a consistent perceived oblique screen direction (e.g., side to center) across two reverse shots, the actor's actual physical direction of movement in the second shot can be deliberately altered or 'cheated' to match the screen direction established in the first shot.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character's diagonal movement is covered by reverse angles, and the natural physical reversal of the second camera position would cause a confusing or undesired change in perceived screen direction, thus requiring a subtle 'cheat' to maintain visual flow.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience perceives a smooth, continuous diagonal movement across the cut, avoiding disorientation or jarring transitions despite a subtle alteration in the actor's physical path, thereby maintaining narrative immersion.
theory_units.caution: This technique involves deliberately changing the actor's real movement path in the second shot to maintain screen continuity. It requires careful blocking and clear communication with the performer to achieve the desired visual effect without looking unnatural.

theory_units.title: Common Visual Axis: Forward Cut for Approaching Movement
theory_units.summary: To cover a player moving away from the foreground towards a distant position, place two cameras on the same visual axis. Cut on action from a wider shot (covering most of the path) to a closer shot (forward on the same axis) to show the completion of the movement, maintaining the player's screen sector.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character is moving away from the camera, and the director wants to maintain a strong sense of direct visual continuity while also advancing the viewer closer to the subject's destination or final position without changing their apparent screen direction.
theory_units.expected_effect: A seamless, continuous movement that draws the audience further into the scene along the character's path, emphasizing the distance covered and the destination, creating a sense of progression and intimacy.
theory_units.caution: Careful execution is needed for the cut on action to be smooth and invisible. The player must move in the same screen sector in both shots (e.g., always from right to center) to maintain visual consistency.

theory_units.title: Common Visual Axis: Two Players Moving Away & Converging
theory_units.summary: Apply the common visual axis technique to two players moving away together by cutting from a wider shot (establishing the initial group or context) to a closer shot on the same axis. This focuses on the moving pair, emphasizing their interaction or subsequent actions after their initial departure.
theory_units.applies_when: When two characters initiate movement together from a larger group or static position, and the scene transitions to focus specifically on their subsequent interaction or actions as they move away.
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamlessly transitions the audience's focus from a wider group shot to a closer, more intimate view of the moving pair, highlighting their departure and subsequent interaction without breaking spatial continuity or flow.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the distance covered is appropriate for the cut, as described in the example (e.g., short distance with specific step counts mentioned).

theory_units.title: Common Visual Axis: Backward Cut for Receding Movement
theory_units.summary: To emphasize a player's increasing distance, isolation, or integration into a larger environment as they walk away, cut from a medium shot to a long shot, both positioned on the same visual axis, while maintaining the player's centrality in the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character is moving away from the camera, and the narrative intent is to convey their growing physical distance, sense of loneliness, vulnerability, or to emphasize the vastness of the setting engulfing them.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience perceives the character receding further into the environment, emphasizing their growing distance, potential isolation, or the expanding scale of their surroundings, thereby creating a specific emotional or contextual impact.
theory_units.caution: Maintain the player's centrality in both shots to ensure the visual connection along the common axis and prevent jarring shifts in composition.

theory_units.title: Continuous Movement - Subject Walks Away and Stops
theory_units.summary: A subject moving away from the camera in a medium shot transitions to a full shot, completing their movement by taking a few steps in the new shot and stopping centrally.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a character's continuous movement where they walk away from the camera towards another character or a destination and stop.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a smooth transition while emphasizing the character's arrival and the conclusion of their initial movement, often relating them to their environment or another character.
theory_units.caution: The subject must conclude their movement quickly (1-2 steps) and centrally in the second shot for a natural feel.

theory_units.title: Subject Concludes Movement Centrally at Cut
theory_units.summary: When cutting between shots that maintain a common visual axis, the mobile subject should conclude their movement at the beginning of the second shot, moving only one or two steps and stopping at the screen's center.
theory_units.applies_when: Transitioning between two shots (e.g., Full Shot to Medium Shot, Medium Shot to Full Shot) that cover a continuous movement along a common visual axis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures a smooth and visually coherent cut, making the subject's destination and the completion of their action clear.
theory_units.caution: Movement must be minimal (1-2 steps) and conclude centrally to avoid an awkward or prolonged stop.

theory_units.title: Approaching Movement - Revealing Surroundings
theory_units.summary: A subject approaching the camera in a full shot transitions to another full shot on the same visual axis, continuing their approach and stopping in the foreground, expanding the view to include their surroundings.
theory_units.applies_when: A character or vehicle is approaching the camera, and the director wants to emphasize their journey, arrival, and relationship to their environment.
theory_units.expected_effect: Widening the audience's view in the second shot, creating a visual 'need' to see the subject's surroundings, identifying the player, and revealing their intentions/feelings.
theory_units.caution: Cut when the subject 'crowds' the frame, meaning their head reaches the top boundary, but not so much as to obscure the view completely.

theory_units.title: Contrasting Camera Angles for Approaching Movement
theory_units.summary: When covering an approaching movement across two shots on a common visual axis, the second shot can use a higher or lower camera position to contrast with a level first shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Desiring to add visual interest or subtle emphasis to a continuous approaching movement across a cut.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides visual contrast and can subtly alter the audience's perception of the approaching subject (e.g., low angle for power, high angle for vulnerability).
theory_units.caution: Ensure the chosen angle serves the narrative or emotional intent and maintains visual continuity.

theory_units.title: Initiating Departure with Screen Sector Repetition
theory_units.summary: To show the beginning of a walking movement, a close shot depicts a character looking off-screen and starting to move diagonally towards the screen edge. A cut then reveals them in a full shot, further back on the same visual axis, continuing the diagonal movement in the same screen zone.
theory_units.applies_when: Showing a character's initial decision or intention to depart, emphasizing the beginning of their movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a clear sense of intention and a smooth, amplified depiction of the character's departure from a specific screen sector.
theory_units.caution: The diagonal movement and screen sector repetition must be carefully matched between shots for a smooth transition.

theory_units.title: Arrival at Destination - Approaching Figure Meets Static Subject
theory_units.summary: A sequence showing a figure approaching a static subject uses a medium shot to establish the static subject and the approaching figure, then cuts to a close shot (forward on the same visual axis) of the static subject with the approaching figure arriving in the foreground.
theory_units.applies_when: Depicting the arrival of one character to meet another, emphasizing the arrival and the interaction point.
theory_units.expected_effect: Focuses audience attention on the moment of arrival and the interaction between the characters.
theory_units.caution: Consider pacing: the text implies that the first two-thirds of the movement might be shown in a wider shot, with the remainder in the closer shot, suggesting careful shot scale choice for pacing.

theory_units.title: Discontinuous Motion Covered by Repeated Shots & Cut-Away
theory_units.summary: A discontinuous action sequence can be covered by repeating a pair of shots (on a common visual axis) separated by a cut-away, with character movement utilizing different screen sectors in each repetition.
theory_units.applies_when: Filming a character performing a multi-part action that includes a pause for observation or a break in continuous movement, wanting to emphasize spatial relationships and character perception.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dynamic portrayal of the action, highlights moments of pause/observation, and establishes the character's interaction with their environment. The repetitive motion within screen sectors can create a rhythmic feel.
theory_units.caution: Careful matching of movement direction and screen sector use between repetitions is crucial for clarity and continuity.

theory_units.title: Manipulating Time and Place with Cut-Aways
theory_units.summary: Intercutting shots of a character with a cut-away to another location can make two geographically distant locations appear to be the same place and time, allowing filmmakers to utilize outstanding locations regardless of their proximity.
theory_units.applies_when: When practical reasons necessitate filming in geographically distant but visually similar locations, or to create a sense of unified space for narrative purposes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamlessly blends different locations into a cohesive narrative space, enhances production value by leveraging diverse locations, and maintains narrative flow.
theory_units.caution: The 'situation being shot' must allow for this manipulation, implying that the visual coherence and narrative justification are crucial for audience acceptance.

theory_units.title: Diagonal Movement Across Half Screen Areas
theory_units.summary: A diagonal movement across the screen can be covered by using two shots on a common visual axis, with each shot utilizing half of the screen area for the subject's movement before cutting.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing a character's diagonal journey across a space, emphasizing progression from background to foreground or vice versa.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dynamic and clear representation of diagonal movement, breaking it down into manageable visual segments.
theory_units.caution: Precise matching of the character's position at the cut point, particularly when they reach the screen center, is essential for a smooth transition.

theory_units.title: Right Angle Camera Sites for Enhanced Motion Span
theory_units.summary: Utilizing right angle camera sites enhances the perception of motion by allowing coverage over a larger span of terrain, combining across-the-screen, diagonal, or neutral direction movements.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing character movement across a significant area, aiming to make the movement feel expansive and dynamic.
theory_units.expected_effect: Makes movement feel more extensive and dynamic compared to common visual axis setups, providing greater visual interest and spatial information.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful consideration of the cut point and matching of the subject's position for smooth transitions, as right angle cuts can be jarring if not executed precisely.

theory_units.title: Right Angle Coverage - Motion by Halves of Screen Space
theory_units.summary: This technique covers a character's movement by using two shots from right angle camera positions. The first shot shows the player moving across one half of the screen, and the second shot shows them moving diagonally in the other half area of the picture frame.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing a character's continuous movement that needs to be covered across different screen sections and directions, using right-angle camera setups.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually breaks down a complex or long movement into clear segments, using the dynamic shifts of right-angle perspectives.
theory_units.caution: Precise matching of the subject's position at the cut (e.g., at the center of the screen) is important to maintain flow and continuity.

theory_units.title: Right Angle Coverage - Movement Within Screen Boundaries
theory_units.summary: To cover a long trajectory of a performer moving without leaving the screen boundaries, use two shots with a right-angle relationship, where the second shot features neutral direction motion.
theory_units.applies_when: A character needs to traverse a significant distance within a scene without exiting the frame, and the director wants to create a sense of continuous journey through spatial shifts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a smooth and extended sense of movement despite the character remaining within the frame, using the shift in camera perspective.
theory_units.caution: A critical condition for a smooth cut is that 'the end of Shot 1 and beginning of Shot 2 are on the same picture area'. If the moving figure is not precisely positioned, the cut will not be smooth.

theory_units.title: Right Angle Coverage - Reversing Approaching/Receding Movement
theory_units.summary: The shot order in right angle coverage can be reversed to cover an approaching movement instead of a receding one, with the cut point often at the screen's center.
theory_units.applies_when: Adapting existing right-angle movement patterns to depict a character approaching the camera or audience, rather than moving away.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows for flexible narrative direction (arrival vs. departure) using similar camera setups, maintaining visual continuity.
theory_units.caution: The player in motion must maintain the same screen size on both shots at the moment of the cut. Discrepancies in the size of the subject on the cut will render it awkward.

theory_units.title: Match Cut Rule - Consistent Subject Screen Size
theory_units.summary: When cutting between shots involving a moving subject, particularly in right-angle or changing shot size transitions, the subject must maintain the same screen size at the moment of the cut for a smooth transition.
theory_units.applies_when: Any cut where a moving subject is present in both shots, especially when changing shot size or camera angle significantly.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures a seamless and visually pleasing transition, preventing jarring jumps or awkward changes in the subject's size.
theory_units.caution: Discrepancies in the size of the subject on the cut will render it awkward and break continuity for the audience.

theory_units.title: Right Angle Coverage - Subject Appears from Behind Foreground Performer
theory_units.summary: When a neutral movement in the first shot ends, a cut to a right-angle side shot can show the subject appearing from behind a foreground performer, shortening their horizontal motion. The sequence can be reversed for the subject leaving.
theory_units.applies_when: Introducing a character into a scene where other performers are already present, or when a character is leaving an interaction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a natural and integrated entrance/exit for the character, using foreground elements to establish their position and reduce unnecessary horizontal movement.
theory_units.caution: Careful blocking and timing are needed for the subject to appear naturally from behind the foreground performer and for the match cut to be smooth.

theory_units.title: Fixed Aperture Framing for Fragmented Motion
theory_units.summary: A fixed aperture (like a door frame) seen in the first shot can frame the second part of a fragmented motion in the second shot, where the subject enters through the aperture.
theory_units.applies_when: A character is moving towards or through a doorway or similar architectural feature, and the director wants to emphasize the transition between spaces.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly defines the transition of the character into a new space, uses environmental framing for visual interest, and maintains the central placement of movement.
theory_units.caution: The position of the aperture relative to the camera in Shot 1 influences the character's appearance direction in Shot 2, requiring careful planning for screen direction.

theory_units.title: Oblique Approach - Matching with Side Shot
theory_units.summary: If a subject's approach in the first shot is oblique, the second shot must be placed on the same side of the line of motion and can be a side shot, using the screen's center to match the movement.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing a character's diagonal movement towards an interaction or a specific point, needing a smooth transition to a closer view.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains smooth visual continuity for oblique movement by ensuring camera placement respects the line of action, and clarifies the character's arrival or position.
theory_units.caution: The 'same side of the line of motion' rule is critical for maintaining screen direction and continuity, preventing disorientation for the audience.

theory_units.title: Right Angle Coverage for Relating Set Areas
theory_units.summary: Using right-angle camera positions to cover a character's movement, thereby visually connecting two different areas of the set.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character's movement needs to link or transition between distinct geographical areas within a set.
theory_units.expected_effect: Relates two different areas of the set; provides a sense of character progression through space.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Central Action Across Varied Scales
theory_units.summary: Confining a character's action to the central sector of the screen across multiple cuts, even when using drastically different shot sizes (e.g., full shot to long shot).
theory_units.applies_when: When showing continuous action across various shot scales, particularly when the subject may appear very small, to maintain audience focus.
theory_units.expected_effect: Facilitates audience tracking of the action, making it easy to follow the subject despite changes in their perceived size on screen.

theory_units.title: Movement Across Screen for Arrival/Departure
theory_units.summary: Utilizing horizontal character movement across the screen, within the picture boundaries, as a visual cue to show a performer's arrival or departure in continuous action.
theory_units.applies_when: When joining fragments of a continuous action to signify a character entering or leaving the scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clear and continuous depiction of a character's entry or exit.

theory_units.title: Match Cut Panning to Static for Across-Screen Movement
theory_units.summary: A technique to smoothly unite a panning shot and a static camera shot by matching the performer's body position at the cut point, often used to conclude an across-the-screen motion.
theory_units.applies_when: When transitioning from a dynamic panning shot to a static shot for an across-screen movement, especially to bring the motion to a close.
theory_units.expected_effect: Smooth continuity between a moving and static camera, providing a clear conclusion to the character's motion.

theory_units.title: Horizontal Motion Across Opposed Screen Sectors
theory_units.summary: Filming horizontal motion using camera positions that place the character in opposed screen sectors (e.g., center-to-right then left-to-center) while maintaining the same overall sense of direction.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting continuous horizontal movement using varied framing across cuts, aiming for dynamic visual progression.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains continuous horizontal motion across cuts using varied screen space.

theory_units.title: Repeating Movement for Arrival/Departure Conclusion
theory_units.summary: A variation where a character's movement is repeated across a small sector (e.g., central third) of the screen in a closer shot to conclude an arrival or departure sequence.
theory_units.applies_when: To emphasize and conclude the final segment of a character's arrival or departure, providing a clear endpoint.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the completion of movement, providing a clear visual end to the action.

theory_units.title: Reverse Angle Motion for Dynamic Departure/Arrival
theory_units.summary: Utilizing external reverse angles or a combination of external-internal angles for across-screen movement, intentionally resulting in divergent screen directions between shots for a more dynamic effect.
theory_units.applies_when: When a dynamic visual effect is desired for a character's departure or arrival, consciously breaking strict screen direction for impact.
theory_units.expected_effect: A more dynamic screen presentation; can create a sense of abruptness or heightened emphasis on the transition.
theory_units.caution: Can break the principle of constant screen direction and cause abrupt shifts in the center of interest if the character is profiled throughout both shots.

theory_units.title: Mitigating Profiled Reverse Angle Conflicts
theory_units.summary: To smooth the transition between conflicting reverse angle shots involving profiled characters, introduce a neutral direction of motion or a pause between the shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When using reverse angle cuts for characters in profiled positions where the opposed screen directions would otherwise create a jarring, discontinuous effect.
theory_units.expected_effect: Smoother passage between shots despite opposed directions, maintaining the feeling of continuous movement and constant screen direction.
theory_units.caution: Failure to apply this with profiled characters can lead to an abrupt shift of the center of interest and a broken sense of screen direction.

theory_units.title: Match Cut on Limb Movement for Incompatible Views
theory_units.summary: Using a significant, continuous limb movement as a match cut point to smoothly unite two otherwise incompatible reverse camera views of two players, even if their screen positions reverse.
theory_units.applies_when: Transitioning between reverse camera views of two characters involved in a physical action (e.g., a slap), where maintaining continuous action is paramount over strict spatial continuity.
theory_units.expected_effect: A smooth and seemingly continuous cut, masking abrupt switches in screen area for subjects by emphasizing the ongoing action.

theory_units.title: Regular Doorway Crossing: Maintaining Screen Direction
theory_units.summary: For a character passing through a doorway, positioning cameras for both interior and exterior shots on the same side of the imaginary line of movement to ensure continuous screen direction.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character crosses a threshold (e.g., a doorway) and maintaining clear, continuous screen direction is desired for audience orientation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamless and continuous movement through the doorway, preserving audience's spatial understanding and preventing disorientation.

theory_units.title: Irregular Doorway Crossing: Dynamic Opposed Directions
theory_units.summary: Consciously choosing an 'irregular' treatment for a doorway crossing by placing camera sites on opposite sides of the line of action, resulting in opposed screen directions for a more dynamic effect.
theory_units.applies_when: When a dynamic, potentially jarring, or emphasized transition through a doorway is desired, especially if the door is open in both shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: A more dynamic and impactful screen transition; can create a sense of abruptness or shift in energy.
theory_units.caution: This approach intentionally breaks strict screen direction, which might be disorienting if not used purposefully.

theory_units.title: Time Compression for Non-Dramatic Movement
theory_units.summary: To efficiently compress time, omit the middle portion of a character's movement that holds no dramatic value, showing only the beginning and conclusion.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character's movement, such as crossing a threshold, is not dramatically significant and time needs to be condensed.
theory_units.expected_effect: Accelerated scene pacing, efficient storytelling, audience focus on key dramatic moments.

theory_units.title: Stressing Dramatic Door Opening
theory_units.summary: In a dramatic situation, delay the opening of a door for as long as possible without compromising scene effectiveness, to emphasize its significance.
theory_units.applies_when: When the act of opening a door carries significant dramatic weight or is a key turning point.
theory_units.expected_effect: Heightened tension, increased audience anticipation, emphasis on the dramatic importance of the moment.
theory_units.caution: Avoid delaying to the point of harming scene effectiveness or audience frustration.

theory_units.title: Masking Direction Change with Static Door Shot
theory_units.summary: Use a static shot of a closed door from the inside, held for 1-2 seconds, as a visual pause after a character's approach/knock and before their entry, to mask a change in their movement direction.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character enters a closed door and an unmotivated change in their movement direction between shots needs to be smoothly masked.
theory_units.expected_effect: Smooths transitions, prevents audience confusion regarding screen direction, provides a moment of anticipation.

theory_units.title: Centering Moving Player for Screen Position Continuity
theory_units.summary: To prevent screen position reversal when one player approaches a waiting player near a door, keep the moving player centered in both shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a scene with a moving player approaching a stationary player near a threshold, where a cut might otherwise reverse screen positions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains audience orientation, avoids confusing screen direction jumps for the moving player, allows the stationary player's position to shift without confusion.
theory_units.caution: This technique focuses on the moving player's continuity, allowing the stationary player's screen position to change.

theory_units.title: Establishing Communication Through a Barrier
theory_units.summary: When two players communicate through an opaque barrier, use shots in opposed directions with opposing eye lines to visually establish their connection and rapport.
theory_units.applies_when: When portraying two characters speaking to each other through a physical barrier (e.g., a closed door) that prevents direct visual contact.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a visual sense of communication, connection, and rapport between the separated characters for the audience.

theory_units.title: Fragmenting Continuous Motion
theory_units.summary: Break down any continuous motion into at least two visual fragments for effective editing and presentation.
theory_units.applies_when: Whenever a character, animal, or vehicle performs a continuous movement across a space or within a scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enables dynamic editing, allows for time compression or expansion, permits changes in perspective, and helps manage complex actions.

theory_units.title: Match-on-Action Cutting
theory_units.summary: Ensure cuts between shots occur precisely on the action itself to maintain continuity and create fluid, imperceptible transitions.
theory_units.applies_when: When editing any continuous movement that spans across multiple shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Smooth, invisible cuts that maintain audience engagement and prevent jarring discontinuities.

theory_units.title: Varying Shot Distance in Motion Edits
theory_units.summary: Involve a change in camera-to-subject distance when cutting between fragments of a continuous motion.
theory_units.applies_when: When editing continuous movement across multiple shots to add visual interest and vary emphasis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds visual dynamism, changes emphasis (e.g., from context to detail), helps disguise cuts, and provides new information or perspective.

theory_units.title: Triangle Principle for Camera Placement (Motion)
theory_units.summary: Utilize variants of the triangle principle for camera placement (reverse shots, right angles, common visual axis) to effectively register broken action, for both on-the-spot and along-a-path movements.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a character's movement across multiple shots to ensure spatial and directional clarity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains consistent screen direction, provides diverse angles while preserving spatial continuity, ensures logical relationships between subjects and environment.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful adherence to the 180-degree rule and its deliberate exceptions to avoid disorientation.

theory_units.title: Screen Sector Composition for Action
theory_units.summary: For filming action fragments, divide the screen into two or three sectors, ensuring that each shot primarily covers one designated sector.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing individual shots that are part of a larger continuous action sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates structured compositions, directs audience attention, efficiently manages screen space, and aids in maintaining continuity across cuts.

theory_units.title: Screen Sector Repetition for Dynamic Movement
theory_units.summary: When presenting dynamic continuous movement split into two half-screen shots, repeat the motion within the same screen sector, either in the same or opposed directions.
theory_units.applies_when: When editing continuous movement across two shots, specifically utilizing half-screen areas for compositional balance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains visual consistency or creates a dynamic contrast, guides the viewer's eye, and reinforces the continuous nature of the movement.

theory_units.title: Movement Start/End Points in Frame
theory_units.summary: For continuous movement across shots, ensure the movement either begins and ends in the screen's center, or starts on one side and concludes on the opposite side.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing shots for continuous movement, particularly when editing between them.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides clear visual anchors, maintains spatial understanding for the audience, and creates a sense of purposeful progression or completion.

theory_units.title: Converging/Diverging Motion Composition
theory_units.summary: Compose continuous motion either to converge towards the center of the screen or to diverge from it.
theory_units.applies_when: When designing the visual path of a continuous movement within a shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates visual tension or focus (convergence), or a sense of release, expansion, or departure (divergence); emphasizes the subject's journey or destination.

theory_units.title: Movement Inside the Screen (Economy)
theory_units.summary: To achieve economy and dynamism, compose continuous movement so the subject does not fully exit the screen in the first shot but enters in the second, suggesting motion without full exit/entry.
theory_units.applies_when: When an economical, dynamic, and effective suggestion of motion is desired across a cut, without requiring the subject to fully leave and re-enter the frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: More effective and economical suggestion of motion, leading to fast and dynamic shot-to-shot transitions.
theory_units.caution: This is a preference and alternative to the 'motion into and out of shot' technique.

theory_units.title: Subject Re-entry Options (Motion Out of Shot)
theory_units.summary: When a subject exits a shot, they can either re-enter from the opposite side in the subsequent shot, or already be in view (center or side) in the next shot.
theory_units.applies_when: When employing the 'motion into and out of shot' technique for continuous movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains spatial continuity, establishes new position or context, or implies passage of time/distance depending on the re-entry method.

theory_units.title: Cutting on Subject Exit
theory_units.summary: When a subject moves out of frame, the cut can occur either when the subject is partially out of frame, or the shot can be held for a few frames after their complete exit.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character or object exits the frame as part of a continuous movement sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Controls pacing, creates anticipation for the next shot, or provides a brief moment of stillness/aftermath following the motion.
theory_units.caution: Choosing between partial exit cut and holding the shot affects pacing and viewer emphasis.

theory_units.title: Cutting on Subject Entry
theory_units.summary: For subjects entering the screen, the cutting techniques are generally the reverse of those for exiting subjects.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character or object enters the frame as part of a continuous movement sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Controls the revelation of the character/object, establishes their presence or new scene context, and affects scene pacing.

theory_units.title: Fragmenting Long Repetitive Motion
theory_units.summary: Break long, repetitive movements into three or four fragments, or insert a cut-away, to shorten it without confusing the audience and prevent weakening the story.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a lengthy, repetitive movement that lacks significant dramatic meaning or detail.
theory_units.expected_effect: Compresses narrative time, maintains audience engagement, avoids boredom, keeps the story focused on essential elements.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the fragmentation or cut-away does not confuse the audience about the continuity of the action.

theory_units.title: Justifying Lengthy Repetitive Motion
theory_units.summary: Only retain a lengthy repetitive motion in its entirety if it can be endowed with significant visual qualities that justify its screen time, otherwise it risks weakening the story.
theory_units.applies_when: When considering whether to show a full, lengthy, and potentially repetitive movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures all screen time is dramatically or aesthetically justified, preventing audience disengagement or boredom.
theory_units.caution: Justifying such motion may sometimes require a forced or contrived mise en scene.

theory_units.title: Blending Locations with Motion Out/In
theory_units.summary: A subject moving out of the screen in one shot and entering it in the next naturally blends separate locations, creating a convincing transition between two disparate areas.
theory_units.applies_when: When transitioning between two geographically separate locations while maintaining the continuity of a character's movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a seamless and natural transition, making disparate locations appear to coexist or be in close proximity.

theory_units.title: Three-Fragment Parallel Camera Coverage (Movement)
theory_units.summary: Cover a continuous movement from one area to another using three camera sites positioned parallel to the subject's path, framing them at a consistent distance.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting a complete, continuous movement across a significant space, aiming for clear spatial representation and smooth transitions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a clear depiction of the journey, maintains consistent scale, and offers a straightforward visual flow of the action.

theory_units.title: Half-Full-Half Screen Sequence (Parallel Movement)
theory_units.summary: A three-shot sequence for continuous movement: 1) half-screen motion exiting, 2) full-screen traverse entering from opposite side and exiting, 3) half-screen motion entering from opposite side and stopping in center.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a continuous movement across a space using three parallel camera sites to clearly record the entire path.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly records the entire path traveled, provides dynamic visual flow, and maintains strong screen direction.

theory_units.title: Three-Fragment Triangular Camera Disposition (Movement)
theory_units.summary: Modify three-fragment movement coverage by moving the center camera backward to create a triangular disposition, with all three cameras pointing straight ahead, for a more dramatic effect.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a continuous movement across a space where a more dramatic or varied visual effect is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased dramatic tension, varied perspective on the journey, emphasizes the journey's length or the destination's significance.

theory_units.title: Center Camera Framing Options (Triangular Movement)
theory_units.summary: In a three-fragment triangular movement coverage, the center camera can frame the space between departure/arrival, intermediate space with arrival/departure zones, or the entire space.
theory_units.applies_when: When using a triangular camera disposition for multi-fragment movement and needing to define the emphasis of the middle shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides context for the journey, reveals progress, or establishes the entire spatial relationship between the start, middle, and end points.

theory_units.title: Close-Full-Close Shot Sequence (Triangular Movement)
theory_units.summary: A three-shot sequence for triangular movement coverage: close shots for departure/arrival (first/last), and a middle full shot showing the performer entering and walking to the center, revealing the destination.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a performer changing zones, specifically to emphasize the beginning and end of the movement while re-establishing the next zone.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly shows zone changes, provides a sense of journey, and the middle shot acts as a re-establishing shot, showing the next zone or adjoining zones.

theory_units.title: Three-Sector Screen Division (Central Action)
theory_units.summary: When showing adjoining zones in a single take, divide the screen into three sectors, placing the zones on the left and right, and dedicating the central area for the main performer's action.
theory_units.applies_when: When composing a single shot that needs to simultaneously display both adjoining environmental zones and focus on central character action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides clear spatial context while maintaining focus on the main action, creating a balanced and informative composition.

theory_units.title: Accentuating Violence with Far Viewpoint Cut
theory_units.summary: To accentuate violence depicted in a close shot, cut suddenly to a far away viewpoint.
theory_units.applies_when: After a violent close shot, when the director wants to emphasize its impact or create shock for the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the severity of the violence and creates a jarring or shocking effect on the audience.

theory_units.title: Re-establishing Locale with Central Shot
theory_units.summary: After a sequence of fragmented action, a central shot that includes the full set and intermediate space can effectively re-establish the overall locale for the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: After a series of close-ups or fragmented shots where the audience might lose a sense of the broader location.
theory_units.expected_effect: Re-orients the audience to the physical setting, provides clarity of the overall location, and contextualizes fragmented action.

theory_units.title: Stationary Player's Size to Indicate Movement
theory_units.summary: When a moving player travels past a stationary one along a common visual axis, the stationary player's figure can progressively grow in size across successive shots to implicitly indicate the moving player's spatial progression and the distance covered.
theory_units.applies_when: Showing a character moving past a stationary one, particularly when implying progress or distance covered along a path.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys the moving player's progress and the distance traveled without explicitly showing all of their movement; reinforces spatial progression.

theory_units.title: Screen Zone Repetition (Editing)
theory_units.summary: Join shots of continuous movement by having the moving subject occupy the same screen sector (e.g., right side) at the end of one shot and the beginning of the next.
theory_units.applies_when: Cutting between fragmented shots of a continuous movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a smooth, continuous transition, maintaining a clear sense of the moving subject's direction and position across the cut.

theory_units.title: Action Spot Matching (Editing)
theory_units.summary: Join shots by precisely matching a significant action (e.g., stopping, starting, turning) in the same screen spot across the cut.
theory_units.applies_when: Cutting between fragmented shots, especially when a precise action needs to be emphasized and continuity maintained.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a seamless and strong sense of continuity, drawing focus to the matched action and making the cut less noticeable.
theory_units.caution: Requires precise timing and framing during production and editing.

theory_units.title: Juxtaposing Locations through Fragmented Motion
theory_units.summary: Fragmenting a continuous motion across shots with different camera relationships (e.g., right-angle, common axis) can create the illusion that two distinct locations are spatially side-by-side or closely connected.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to show a character moving between two distinct but implicitly proximate locations, or to visually connect disparate spaces.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a powerful spatial illusion, connecting separate locations in the audience's mind as if they are geographically close, enhancing narrative flow.
theory_units.caution: Careful planning of camera angles and movement is crucial for the illusion to work effectively.

theory_units.title: Limit on Motion Fragmentation
theory_units.summary: Fragmenting a single continuous motion into more than four or five sections typically becomes annoying for the audience and defeats the purpose of conveying movement efficiently.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning to fragment a continuous motion sequence for efficiency or emphasis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents audience frustration and maintains narrative flow; ensures the fragmentation serves its intended purpose rather than becoming disruptive.
theory_units.caution: Avoid exceeding 4-5 cuts for a single continuous motion unless for highly specific artistic or dramatic effect (e.g., extreme stylized violence, rapid montage).

theory_units.title: Suggesting Distance/Path Length (Editing Efficiency)
theory_units.summary: The goal of editing motion, especially for long paths, is to suggest the length of the path traveled without showing the full, tedious movement, which can tire the audience and slow down the story.
theory_units.applies_when: A character needs to travel a significant distance, but the act of traveling itself is not dramatically critical.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains audience engagement, ensures efficient storytelling, and conveys the sense of distance without unnecessary screen time or boredom.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful selection of key moments or visual cues to represent the journey effectively.

theory_units.title: Time Contraction (Waiting Player)
theory_units.summary: To compress time and suggest a long journey, use a three-shot sequence: show a moving player leaving in shot 1, then in shot 2 show them small and traversing the space, and finally in shot 3, show the waiting actor alone for several frames before the moving player enters the screen.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to convey a long journey without depicting its full duration, thereby contracting screen time.
theory_units.expected_effect: Efficiently communicates the passage of time and distance covered, preventing audience fatigue while maintaining clarity.
theory_units.caution: The waiting actor's screen time should be carefully calibrated to avoid boredom or confusion.

theory_units.title: Implied Journey Length (Waiting Actor Screen Time)
theory_units.summary: The duration for which a waiting actor is shown alone on screen before the arrival of a moving player directly influences the audience's perception of the length of the path the moving player traveled.
theory_units.applies_when: Using the 'Time Contraction (Waiting Player)' method; wanting to fine-tune the audience's perception of the journey's length or build anticipation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows the director to precisely control how long the implied journey feels to the audience, affecting pacing and anticipation.
theory_units.caution: Too long can be boring; too short can undermine the sense of distance or anticipation.

theory_units.title: Repetitive Motion and Dramatic Value
theory_units.summary: Repetitive motions (e.g., walking, running) generally lack dramatic value when their sole purpose is to depict a character moving from one place to another.
theory_units.applies_when: Deciding whether to show or compress a character's journey; evaluating the dramatic utility of showing continuous repetitive movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Encourages efficient storytelling by avoiding unnecessary screen time for undramatic actions, maintaining audience engagement and narrative focus.
theory_units.caution: Avoid dwelling on repetitive movements unless they are specifically intended to convey character state (e.g., exhaustion, determination), struggle, or thematic meaning.

theory_units.title: Fragmenting Violent/Fast Motion for Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Fast or violent motions can be fragmented into four or five shots to visually stress the inherent violence or speed of the movement itself.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing a scene with fast-paced or violent action that needs to be visually accentuated and made more impactful.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increases the visual impact and intensity of the movement, emphasizing its speed, force, or brutality.
theory_units.caution: Similar to general fragmentation, exceeding 4-5 shots might become confusing rather than impactful unless highly stylized.

theory_units.title: Using Mirrors for Converging Directions
theory_units.summary: Incorporating a mirror into a shot allows the depiction of converging directions of a single action by an approaching player, while simultaneously maintaining the static performer's screen position across cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: Desiring to show complex or converging movement paths, or to create unusual visual arrangements, especially with an approaching and a static character.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates unique visual arrangements, can show multiple perspectives of an action within one frame, and maintains continuity of other elements for the audience.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful blocking and camera placement to manage reflections and potential confusion for the viewer.

theory_units.title: Varying Shot Size (Right Angle Approach)
theory_units.summary: When employing a right-angle camera setup for an approaching player, varying the shot size between takes (e.g., from Full Shot to Medium Shot) adds visual variety and dynamism to the sequence.
theory_units.applies_when: Implementing a right-angle camera setup to show a player approaching another, particularly over a short distance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances visual interest and dynamism, preventing the sequence from feeling static or repetitive while emphasizing spatial progression.
theory_units.caution: Shot size changes should be motivated by the narrative, character's progression, or scene's emotional beats.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Screen Sector (Right Angle Approach)
theory_units.summary: In a right-angle camera setup for an approaching player, the moving player should consistently maintain their movement within the same screen sector (e.g., always moving from right to left across the frame) across cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: Using a right-angle camera setup to depict a player approaching another, ensuring clear spatial continuity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures clear screen direction and smooth visual continuity, preventing audience disorientation and maintaining a coherent sense of space.
theory_units.caution: Deviating from this principle can easily confuse the audience about the player's direction and spatial relationship.

theory_units.title: Panning Shot for Initial Approach
theory_units.summary: A panning shot can be effectively used for the initial stage of an approaching movement, where the actor walks in a straight path tangential to the panning arc, thereby fluidly covering the ground that might otherwise require multiple static shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Showing an actor beginning an approach, especially when wanting to combine the initial movement into a single, fluid shot rather than a series of cuts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a fluid and dynamic sense of initial movement, efficiently covering distance and potentially revealing more of the environment.
theory_units.caution: Overuse of panning can be distracting; ensure the pan has a clear purpose and controlled speed.

theory_units.title: Stationary Character as Camera Pivot
theory_units.summary: Use a stationary character as a pivot point for camera placement, ensuring they remain in the foreground across multiple shots covering another character's movement.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering the movement of one character in relation to a static character, to maintain visual continuity and a clear spatial relationship.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains a visual anchor for the audience, ensuring clarity of spatial relationships and highlighting the moving character's journey relative to the static one.

theory_units.title: Profiling and Back-to-Camera Movement Coverage
theory_units.summary: Cover an actor's movement by showing them profiled to the camera in the first shot, and with their back to the camera in the second shot.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting a character's movement across two shots, offering varied perspectives of their journey's progression.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides comprehensive visual information about the character's movement and direction, engaging the audience with different angles of the action.

theory_units.title: Panning to Conclude Character Movement
theory_units.summary: Apply a camera pan in the second shot of a sequence to follow a character's concluding movement, bringing them to a stop while facing another performer.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character moves away from the camera in a first shot and then arrives to interact with another character in the second, to smooth the transition and highlight their arrival.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a clear visual conclusion to the character's movement, focuses attention on their arrival and the ensuing interaction, and maintains spatial awareness.

theory_units.title: External Reverse Angles for Movement
theory_units.summary: Utilize a set of external reverse camera angles to cover character movement, showing different perspectives of the actor's approach and departure.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a character's movement, such as walking towards the camera in one shot and entering a subsequent shot with their back to the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides dynamic and comprehensive coverage of the movement, clearly indicating direction and progression, and offering varied visual information.

theory_units.title: Close Shot to Introduce Movement
