theory_units.summary: Record the beginning of a character's movement using a close shot to emphasize the initiation of their action.
theory_units.applies_when: When the start of a character's movement is significant and needs to be highlighted, or to provide an improved sense of intimacy before a longer movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws the audience's attention to the character's intent and the precise moment of their action's commencement, adding emphasis.

theory_units.title: Internal Reverse Angles for Path Coverage
theory_units.summary: Employ internal reverse camera angles to provide comprehensive coverage of the entire path traversed by a moving player.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to clearly show the trajectory and progress of a character's movement within a space from multiple perspectives.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances the audience's understanding of the character's journey and spatial relationship within the environment, providing clear visual transitions.

theory_units.title: Common Visual Axis for Movement Clarity
theory_units.summary: Position cameras on a common visual axis to provide clear and easily executable coverage for a player in motion.
theory_units.applies_when: When seeking a straightforward and clear method to cover a character's movement, ensuring visual coherence across cuts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Offers simple execution and clear visual coverage, making the movement easy for the audience to follow and understand spatially.

theory_units.title: Diagonal Motion with Delayed Arrival Point Reveal
theory_units.summary: When a character moves obliquely across the field of vision, reveal the arrival point (another character) only in the second shot, after the moving character has exited and re-entered.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a character's diagonal movement that takes them out of frame, and the destination/interaction partner is meant to be a reveal or secondary focus.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of anticipation or curiosity regarding the destination, emphasizing the moving character's journey before introducing the full context.

theory_units.title: Frontal Approach for Dynamic Action
theory_units.summary: Favor a frontal approach, where the character moves towards the camera, for greater dynamism compared to moving away, especially when advancing to an unseen destination.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting a character's forward movement and desiring to maximize the visual impact and audience engagement with their action or journey.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a more dynamic and engaging visual experience, drawing the audience into the character's journey and amplifying their presence.
theory_units.caution: Movement away from the camera is generally less dynamic and can reduce audience engagement with the character's immediate action.

theory_units.title: Mirror for Duplicated Entrance Effect
theory_units.summary: Incorporate a background mirror in a shot to show a character's entrance twice within the same shot and screen area, first in reflection, then as a real figure.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming for startling or off-beat visual effects, or to emphasize and draw attention to a character's entrance into a scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a unique and visually striking duplication of motion, providing an 'off-beat' feel and potentially highlighting the character's presence or journey.

theory_units.title: Static Character as Visual Pivot Point
theory_units.summary: Utilize a static character as a visual pivot point across multiple shots to relate them visually, particularly when another character crosses beside them and stops beyond.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a character's movement that involves passing by a stationary person, to maintain clear spatial relationships and continuity between shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates strong visual continuity and a clear spatial relationship between the various shots, anchoring the movement around a consistent element.

theory_units.title: Motivating Character Movement with Business
theory_units.summary: Provide characters with 'significant pieces of business' to naturally motivate their movement across cuts and within scenes.
theory_units.applies_when: Whenever a character moves, especially when the movement is split across multiple shots, to make the action purposeful and believable.
theory_units.expected_effect: Makes character movement feel natural, intentional, and integrated into the narrative, adding realism and depth to the performance.

theory_units.title: Three-Part Movement Coverage with Repeated Shot
theory_units.summary: Cover a character's movement in three parts by using the initial camera position for both the beginning and conclusion of the movement, while an intermediate shot covers the central portion.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character's movement involves passing a stationary companion, and a detailed, yet spatially continuous, depiction of their journey is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides comprehensive coverage of the movement, emphasizing the character's progression and their dynamic relationship to a static element over time, while maintaining clear visual reference points.

theory_units.title: Strategic Use of Inserts/Cut-aways
theory_units.summary: Inserts or cut-aways within a master shot can be used to provide a pause in action, emphasize a situation, or facilitate character recognition.
theory_units.applies_when: When a master shot needs enhancement for pacing, to draw audience attention to specific details or emotions, or to introduce character identity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Manages scene pacing, clarifies narrative points, highlights character internal states or reactions, and allows the audience to connect with characters.

theory_units.title: Reverse Shot Insert for Character Reaction
theory_units.summary: Insert a frontal reverse shot into a master shot sequence to clearly show a character's reaction or expression, especially during a pause in their movement.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character stops their movement and is reacting to an object or situation, and their internal state needs to be conveyed clearly to the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a clear and direct view of the character's emotional state or reaction, fostering audience empathy and understanding more effectively than a distant shot.

theory_units.title: Close-up Insert for Character Identification
theory_units.summary: Integrate a close-up insert into a wide master shot sequence to allow the audience to clearly recognize a character initially seen at a small scale.
theory_units.applies_when: When introducing a character from a distance (e.g., extreme long shot) and the director wants to satisfy the audience's urge to identify them before they become involved in further action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Facilitates early audience recognition and connection with the character, satisfying their need to identify the subject and increasing engagement with subsequent actions.

theory_units.title: Master Shot Movement Segmentation & Insert Substitution
theory_units.summary: Break a long movement in a master shot into segments, show the beginning and end in the master, and replace the central segment with a closer insert shot from a different camera angle to inject dynamism or highlight specific action.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering a character's extended movement in a master shot when dynamism, closer detail, or a change of pace is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased dynamism, enhanced sense of action, allows audience to see detail of central movement while preserving environmental context of start/end, and provides visual contrast.
theory_units.caution: Ensure smooth transitions and spatial continuity between master shot segments and the insert. Overuse may disrupt flow.

theory_units.title: Cutting on Startled Movement to Close-up
theory_units.summary: When a character reacts with a startled turn, cut during the movement to a closer shot on the same visual axis to emphasize their emotional reaction.
theory_units.applies_when: A character experiences a sudden, startled reaction, especially involving a turning movement, and their emotion needs to be highlighted.
theory_units.expected_effect: Heightens the sense of surprise and emphasizes the character's emotional state, while maintaining spatial continuity.
theory_units.caution: Maintain a consistent visual axis to avoid disorienting the audience.

theory_units.title: Cutting on Partial Screen Exit for Movement Continuity
theory_units.summary: To maintain a sense of continuous movement or transition, cut to a wider shot when a character's head is halfway out of the screen during movement towards or across the camera.
theory_units.applies_when: A character is moving towards or across the camera, and a transition to a wider, establishing shot is desired while preserving the flow of motion.
theory_units.expected_effect: Smooth and continuous transition, maintains audience focus on the character's movement, creates anticipation, or effectively reveals the environment.

theory_units.title: Reaction Shot on Approach
theory_units.summary: When one character approaches another, cut to a side close shot of the second character to reveal their reaction to the approach.
theory_units.applies_when: A character is approaching another, and the reaction or emotional state of the approached character is dramatically significant.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the psychological impact of the approach on the receiving character, builds tension, or establishes intimacy.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Sound Level for Impending Menace
theory_units.summary: Varying sound levels, specifically increasing sound during dynamic inserts and decreasing it for calmer master shots, or introducing contrasting sound elements, can accentuate feelings of impending or latent menace.
theory_units.applies_when: Building tension or a sense of impending danger, especially when intercutting between different shot types or levels of action, or setting a mood of latent threat.
theory_units.expected_effect: Heightens audience anxiety and sense of threat, significantly contributes to the scene's overall mood and dramatic impact.
theory_units.caution: Overuse may desensitize the audience; use purposefully and with nuanced variations.

theory_units.title: Parallel Editing of Master Shots for Dramatic Possibilities
theory_units.summary: Edit multiple master shots in parallel to cover a performer's movement, thereby stressing various dramatic possibilities (e.g., external threat, internal feelings) and building excitement, suspense, or action for the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering a character's movement through a dramatically charged environment, especially when multiple points of view, simultaneous threats, or internal emotions need to be conveyed.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates excitement, suspense, or action by showing different facets of the dramatic situation simultaneously or in quick succession, intensifying the audience's emotional engagement.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful staging and clear visual storytelling to avoid audience confusion or disorientation.

theory_units.title: Establishing Extreme Zones of Movement
theory_units.summary: Use initial shots in a sequence to clearly establish the starting point (e.g., hiding place) and the end goal (e.g., target) of a character's significant movement.
theory_units.applies_when: Beginning a sequence involving a character moving a significant distance or towards a specific objective, particularly if the journey itself is central to the drama.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides immediate spatial and narrative clarity, sets up the stakes of the movement, and gives the audience a clear understanding of the character's journey and objective.

theory_units.title: Suspenseful Pay-off Intercutting
theory_units.summary: Build suspense by foreshadowing a critical danger, delaying its immediate consequence, and then intercutting to the 'pay-off' shot (e.g., the threat materializing) at a crucial moment to confirm the danger was real, but the hero narrowly escaped.
theory_units.applies_when: Creating a high-stakes moment where a previously established threat is about to materialize, and the hero is on the verge of being discovered or caught.
theory_units.expected_effect: Intensifies audience tension, provides a thrilling 'nick of time' escape, validates prior narrative warnings, and reinforces the hero's vulnerability or luck.
theory_units.caution: The prior setup and clear communication of the danger to the audience are essential for the pay-off to be effective and impactful.

theory_units.title: Visual Pause for Smooth Direction Change
theory_units.summary: When a performer moves between zones with opposed dominant centers, a brief visual pause at the beginning of the second shot, where the moving player is momentarily excluded, allows the audience to reorient to a new camera position and masks the change of direction.
theory_units.applies_when: A performer needs to move between two distinct zones of interest that would otherwise result in an awkward camera position (e.g., facing the rear of a static subject) or an abrupt direction change.
theory_units.expected_effect: A smooth, less jarring transition for the audience when there's a significant shift in camera perspective or character direction, preventing confusion and maintaining coherence.
theory_units.caution: This solution may lead to an unavoidable reversal of screen zone position for both main players in some cases (as noted for Fig 15.2).

theory_units.title: Direct Cut with Right Angle Coverage for Converging Motion
theory_units.summary: Instead of a visual pause, a direct cut can be used with right-angle camera coverage when fragmented motion converges on the screen's center, especially if the movement in one shot occupies a narrow central area.
theory_units.applies_when: Two persons are meeting, or one performer is helping another, and their movements naturally converge towards the center of the screen across two shots taken at right angles, allowing for the omission of a visual pause.
theory_units.expected_effect: A visually interesting and smooth transition that emphasizes the convergence of movement, suitable for interactions like meetings or assistance, without needing a pause.

theory_units.title: Fragmented Motion with Reverse Angles (Static/Moving Dynamic)
theory_units.summary: When one player is static (e.g., seated) and another standing player moves to emphasize a point, their motion can be fragmented across opposed halves of the screen using reverse angles.
theory_units.applies_when: One character, typically standing, needs to move dramatically between sides of a static character (e.g., seated) to make a point or shift focus, using reverse angles.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the moving player's action and intent by segmenting their motion and presenting it from contrasting perspectives, maintaining directional coherence.
theory_units.caution: The speed factor is very important and must be considered.

theory_units.title: Perceived Motion Speed Adjustment via Shot Size
theory_units.summary: Using a close shot for the second half of a fragmented motion increases the perceived speed of the figure, allowing for a swifter traversal of screen area that can cut well with a preceding slower motion, even if the actual movement speed is similar.
theory_units.applies_when: Fragmenting a single motion into two parts where the second part needs to feel more dynamic or quicker, or to visually emphasize the moving figure.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased visual emphasis and a sense of accelerated motion for the character, creating a dynamic contrast with a potentially slower preceding shot.
theory_units.caution: A reversal where perceived speed from shot to shot decreases on a continuous single motion will not work successfully.

theory_units.title: Shot Size Impact on Screen Reversal Visibility
theory_units.summary: The choice of shot size significantly affects how noticeable a screen reversal of players is; close shots make reversals very marked, while long shots diminish their prominence.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning a sequence where players' screen positions reverse, and the director needs to control the audience's awareness or emphasis on this reversal.
theory_units.expected_effect: Close shots strongly emphasize the positional reversal, making it more pronounced. Long shots make the reversal less noticeable, integrating it more subtly into the scene.

theory_units.title: Divergent Motions (Moving Away from Center)
theory_units.summary: A performer can move away from the scene by exiting from the center, using a reverse full shot for the second half of the movement where they complete their exit or turn to face the group.
theory_units.applies_when: A character needs to depart from a group or scene, originating from the center of the frame and moving outwards.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly establishes the character's departure from the scene or group, providing a dynamic exit that can conclude with either an exit or a final interaction with the group.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Constant Screen Position for One Player
theory_units.summary: An irregular variation where one player remains in a constant screen area across shots while another player crosses the screen, often starting with neutral direction movement and then crossing.
theory_units.applies_when: The narrative requires one character to serve as a fixed point of reference while another character's movement is emphasized or charted across the space.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains a stable anchor point in the composition with the static player, allowing the audience to focus on the journey or action of the moving player without feeling disoriented by dual-character movement.

theory_units.title: Both Players Move (Converging Parallel Paths)
theory_units.summary: Both players move on parallel paths in opposite directions, converging on the center, with a cut occurring as their figures are about to overlap, followed by a reverse close shot where they enter from opposite sides and stop facing each other.
theory_units.applies_when: Two characters need to meet and initiate an interaction or dialogue, with their approach being a significant part of the scene's dynamic.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dynamic and fluid sense of convergence, culminating in a focused interaction, with the cut smoothly bridging the approaching movements.
theory_units.caution: The positions of the actors in the second shot are reversed, but their converging motions in each sector of the screen must be identical to work smoothly.

theory_units.title: Reversing Procedures for Departure Motion
theory_units.summary: To cover a character moving away from another, the established procedures for characters moving towards each other can generally be reversed (order of shots, direction of movement) to achieve smooth and varied coverage.
theory_units.applies_when: A character is leaving another, and the director needs to adapt existing techniques for approaching movement to this departing scenario.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides clear and coherent coverage of a character's departure, leveraging established visual grammar for motion towards another character.
theory_units.caution: The triangular camera placement principle still applies.

theory_units.title: Special Effect: Mirrors for Departing Player
theory_units.summary: Using two angled mirrors on screen, a departing player can begin their motion by leaving one mirror and entering the other, with the mirrors acting as 'mini screens' for their movement while a static player remains on the main screen.
theory_units.applies_when: A stylized or unusual visual presentation is desired for a character's departure, potentially to highlight the static character's perspective or to create an artistic effect.
theory_units.expected_effect: A unique, multi-layered visual presentation of departure, creating a sense of fragmented presence for the moving player and constant presence for the static one.

theory_units.title: Departure Motion with Common Visual Axis
theory_units.summary: Two camera positions placed on a common visual axis can be used to film a motion of departure, either across the screen or diagonally towards the camera, with fragments of motion recorded on only one half of the screen in the same sector for both shots.
theory_units.applies_when: A character is departing, and the director wants to maintain a consistent visual axis and screen sector for the fragmented motion.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides smooth and coherent coverage of a character's departure, particularly when the motion is across the screen or diagonally towards the camera, maintaining visual consistency across the cut.

theory_units.title: Departure Motion with Right Angle Camera Placement
theory_units.summary: For a performer's departure, a right-angle camera placement shows both players in the first shot, then only the moving one in the second shot, where they move away in a neutral direction from the screen center.
theory_units.applies_when: A character is departing, and the director uses a right-angle setup to facilitate their exit, with the focus shifting to the departing character alone in the second shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly establishes the character's departure, transitioning the focus to their independent movement as they leave the scene.

theory_units.title: Stationary Player's Point of View (Omission)
theory_units.summary: Omit a stationary player from a subsequent shot to make that shot represent their point of view of a departing player.
theory_units.applies_when: When you want the audience to experience the visual perspective of a stationary character as another character moves away.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience perceives the moving player's position from the perspective of the static player; emphasizes the static player's presence through their absence from the frame.

theory_units.title: Shot Size for Perceived Distance Continuity
theory_units.summary: Adjust the shot size of a departing player in a subsequent shot to correspond to the perceived distance from the static player's viewpoint, matching the initial shot's distance.
theory_units.applies_when: When maintaining visual continuity of perceived distance for a departing player from a stationary character's POV across a cut.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains the illusion of continuous distance traveled by the departing player from the stationary player's perspective.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Rhythm through Shot Size Variation
theory_units.summary: Varying the shot size (e.g., close, far, close) of a moving player across fragmented shots creates a dynamic visual rhythm.
theory_units.applies_when: Fragmenting continuous motion of a player and desiring a dynamic visual rhythm.
theory_units.expected_effect: Confers a dynamic visual rhythm, enhances the sense of fragmentation of motion.

theory_units.title: Panning to Stress Motion (Impersonal POV)
theory_units.summary: Use a camera pan to follow a departing player from a right-angle coverage, creating an impersonal point of view that stresses the player's motion.
theory_units.applies_when: When a player walks away from a companion and the director wants to emphasize the motion itself rather than the emotional impact on a stationary character.
theory_units.expected_effect: Stresses the motion of the departing player, creates an impersonal point of view.
theory_units.caution: This method is 'less emphatic' (emotionally resonant) than using the stationary player's point of view to convey emotion.

theory_units.title: Fragmenting Lengthy Movement
theory_units.summary: Cover lengthy character movements using multiple camera angles and fragmented shots to maintain visual interest and narrative flow.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering lengthy character movements that might otherwise become monotonous.
theory_units.expected_effect: Better management of lengthy movements, maintaining visual interest and dynamism for the audience.

theory_units.title: Movement Towards Camera, Then Within Frame
theory_units.summary: If a departure movement begins by moving towards the camera in the first shot, its continuation in a reverse second shot should occur within the screen boundaries, keeping the player in view.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering a departure where the initial movement is towards the camera, followed by a reverse shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains visual continuity, ensures the moving player remains within the scene for the continuation of their movement.

theory_units.title: Screen Position Transposition with External Reverse Angles
theory_units.summary: Employing external reverse camera angle coverage can transpose players' screen positions, leading to an exchange of screen areas.
theory_units.applies_when: Using external reverse camera angles, particularly when characters' relative screen positions are meant to dynamically shift (e.g., one passing the other).
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dynamic visual exchange of screen areas between players.

theory_units.title: Background Departure with Intercut Master Shots
theory_units.summary: To cover a departure where a performer moves into the background in the first shot and then out of view in the second, use two master shots edited in parallel, alternating between angles.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering a performer's departure where they recede into the background.
theory_units.expected_effect: Conveys the performer moving further away and eventually exiting the scene, maintaining visual continuity.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Motion via Consistent Screen Sector & Intercut Masters
theory_units.summary: Achieve a dynamic quality of motion by consistently recording movement in the same screen sector across shots, combined with a repetitive editing pattern from intercut master shots. Juxtaposing close and medium shots further adds distance contrast.
theory_units.applies_when: Designing a scene (e.g., a farewell) to possess a dynamic quality of motion, especially involving character departure and intercutting.
theory_units.expected_effect: Imparts a dynamic quality of motion on screen, enhanced contrast in distances and engaging visual flow.

theory_units.title: Smooth Flow of Movement (General Principle)
theory_units.summary: Ensure that character movement transitions smoothly from one shot to the next, integrating individual motions within the general design of the sequence.
theory_units.applies_when: Any sequence involving character movement across multiple shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamless visual flow and continuity between shots, preventing jarring transitions.

theory_units.title: Crossing the Line via Dominant Opposing Motion
theory_units.summary: A dominant character's exit-entrance motion, played on opposite sides of the screen, can smoothly override a 'line crossing' where another stationary character is implicitly shifted to a new screen area.
theory_units.applies_when: Needing to implicitly cross the line of action without disorienting the audience, especially when a dominant character has significant movement across the frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Smooth and visually coherent transition across the line, maintaining continuity despite camera repositioning.
theory_units.caution: Requires 'dominant motion' from a character and movement across 'opposite sides of the screen' to be effective.

theory_units.title: Emphasizing Stationary Performer via Reaction Shot
theory_units.summary: When a performer exits the screen, cutting to a close shot of the remaining static performer's facial reactions can emphasize that character and their emotional state.
theory_units.applies_when: A performer leaves the screen, and the director wants to emphasize the remaining static character or their emotional reaction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes the stationary player, making them the key figure; stresses any subsequent movement or emotional beat they make.
theory_units.caution: Reversing the shot order (cutting from static player CU to moving player exiting shot) de-emphasizes both players; the moving player is on screen too briefly, and the static player is framed too far away, reducing emotional impact.

theory_units.title: Contrasting Screen Directions for Retreating Movement
theory_units.summary: Use two external reverse camera sites to capture a retreating movement in contrasting screen directions across different shots, creating a dynamic visual flow.
theory_units.applies_when: Depicting a continuous retreating movement across multiple shots, aiming for visual dynamism and an engaging flow.
theory_units.expected_effect: Dynamic visual flow through contrasting screen directions, enhancing the sense of continuous movement.

theory_units.title: Suggesting Off-Screen Departure via Head Turn
theory_units.summary: A character's off-screen departure can be suggested, rather than explicitly shown, by having a stationary companion turn their head to follow the implied movement.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character exits the frame, and the director wishes to imply their continued movement without showing it directly, focusing instead on the reaction of a remaining character.
theory_units.expected_effect: Implies off-screen movement, draws attention to the reacting character's perspective, creates a sense of unseen continuity.

theory_units.title: Centered Exit and Crossing Behind Stationary Player
theory_units.summary: A character can exit towards the center in a first shot, and then in a subsequent close-up of a static character, re-enter from the opposite side to cross behind them and exit, emphasizing the static character's central position.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering a departure where the moving character passes behind a static character, with the intention to emphasize the static character's central role.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of the moving character's journey across the scene, highlights the central presence of the static character.

theory_units.title: De-emphasizing Moving Player through Background Out-of-Focus
theory_units.summary: To de-emphasize a moving player without losing narrative sense, show them moving in the background and out of focus in a shot that foregrounds another character.
theory_units.applies_when: When a moving player's role or importance needs to be visually deemphasized while maintaining their presence in the scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually de-emphasizes the moving player, highlights the foreground character, maintains narrative continuity and awareness of the background action.

theory_units.title: Disclosing Static Player with Frontal View on Departure
theory_units.summary: Frame a departing player so that as they leave the shot, they reveal a static player in a frontal view, thereby shifting attention dynamically to the static player. This principle applies whether the departing player turns away or towards the camera.
theory_units.applies_when: A character is departing, and the director wants to dynamically shift audience attention to the remaining stationary character, providing a strong visual reveal.
theory_units.expected_effect: Shifts attention dynamically to the static player, providing a clear frontal view and highlighting their presence.

theory_units.title: Shortening Long Movements (Towards Camera) with Pause
theory_units.summary: To shorten long, repetitive character movements towards the camera, cut from the initial action to the destination, placing a pause *before* the character completes their final action in the second shot.
theory_units.applies_when: A character needs to traverse a long distance towards the camera, and the director wants to condense screen time for this movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Makes lengthy travel appear quicker, maintains audience engagement by focusing on key moments rather than repetitive walking.

theory_units.title: Shortening Long Movements (Away From Camera) with Pause
theory_units.summary: When a character departs from the foreground and moves away from the camera over a long path, a pause can be inserted at the conclusion of the *first* shot (remaining with the stationary player) to shorten the perceived travel time.
theory_units.applies_when: A character departs from the foreground and moves away from the camera over a significant distance, and the director wishes to condense the on-screen travel time.
theory_units.expected_effect: Shortens the perceived length of the movement, keeps focus on the remaining character momentarily, and enhances narrative pacing.

theory_units.title: Shortening Long Movements with Visual Distraction
theory_units.summary: To omit a long movement of a departing character towards a visible background destination, introduce a visual distraction in the first shot to momentarily shift audience focus.
theory_units.applies_when: A character needs to traverse a long distance towards a visible destination in the background, and the director wants to shorten this travel time and redirect audience attention.
theory_units.expected_effect: Makes the long movement less noticeable, allows for a more dynamic cut, and redirects audience focus to an active foreground element or character.

theory_units.title: Shortening Long Movements with Related Cut-aways
theory_units.summary: A cut-away shot, directly related to the main action or story, can be inserted between a character's departure and arrival to shorten the perceived distance and time of travel.
theory_units.applies_when: A character needs to traverse a significant distance, and the director wants to compress this travel time while simultaneously providing crucial information or advancing the plot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Shortens travel time, maintains narrative flow, provides vital exposition or plot development, and keeps the audience engaged with relevant information.
theory_units.caution: The cut-away *must* be related to the main action of the story; irrelevant cut-aways will disorient or bore the audience.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Editing for Same-Direction Movement
theory_units.summary: When two characters move in the same direction (one behind the other), a dynamic presentation can be achieved by editing external reverse shots, ensuring screen area repetition and complementary entrances/exits.
theory_units.applies_when: Two characters are moving in the same general direction, one following the other, and the director wants to create a dynamic visual flow through editing.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dynamic and continuous feel for the movement, maintains spatial awareness, and avoids a static or jarring cut.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Entrance from Center for Multiple Characters in Line
theory_units.summary: When cutting to a sequence of characters moving in single file, omitting the entrance of the leading character and having them start their movement from the center of the screen outwards achieves a more dynamic effect.
theory_units.applies_when: Transitioning to a shot of multiple characters moving in a line, particularly when condensing their collective movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a more dynamic visual impact, implies continuous movement, and avoids showing redundant initial steps.
theory_units.caution: Requires an 'almost right angle relationship between the two camera sites'.

theory_units.title: Right Angle Coverage for Multiple Departing Players
theory_units.summary: For multiple players departing in sequence, using a right-angle camera coverage between shots can effectively maintain screen area repetition and show character progression.
theory_units.applies_when: Multiple characters are moving together, one behind the other, and the director needs to cover their departure across multiple shots while maintaining visual continuity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains spatial continuity, shows the progression of multiple characters across the scene, and uses the screen area efficiently.

theory_units.title: Right Angle Coverage for Converging Movement
theory_units.summary: When two players are approaching each other, a right-angle camera coverage can effectively capture their converging movement and meeting.
theory_units.applies_when: Two characters are moving towards each other, and the director wants to capture their convergence effectively across a cut.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly establishes the characters' paths, builds anticipation for their meeting, and maintains spatial logic.

theory_units.title: Common Visual Axis for Converging Movement
theory_units.summary: Covering two players converging on a common visual axis, dividing the first shot into compositional segments and then cutting to a closer shot along the same axis, is an effective method.
theory_units.applies_when: Two characters are moving towards each other along a shared visual line, and the director wants to emphasize their convergence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws the audience's eye along the converging path, intensifies the anticipation of their meeting, and provides a clear spatial relationship.

theory_units.title: Right Angle Coverage for Right-Angle Converging Movement
theory_units.summary: When players converge on paths at right angles to each other, a right-angle camera arrangement effectively captures their movement, attenuating neutral and transverse motions in half-areas of the screen.
theory_units.applies_when: Characters are approaching each other from paths that are perpendicular, and the director wants to clearly show their convergence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly illustrates the right-angle convergence, maintains spatial clarity, and uses screen space dynamically.

theory_units.title: Pacing for Suspense
theory_units.summary: Employing a slow rhythm in a sequence can build tension and emphasize caution or mistrust between characters.
theory_units.applies_when: Characters approach each other with mistrust, or a cautious atmosphere is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates tension, highlights mistrust, emphasizes cautiousness, contributes to dramatic weight.

theory_units.title: Individual Group Descent Introduction
theory_units.summary: When introducing groups descending to meet, first show each group individually with two shots, gradually widening the view to include the terrain, before a re-establishing shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Two or more groups are descending to meet each other, and you want to establish their individual journeys and the environment.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly identifies each group, establishes their movement within the terrain, and builds anticipation for their meeting.

theory_units.title: Close-Up for Character Dominance
theory_units.summary: After establishing two parties, using close shots on key leaders emphasizes their importance and establishes their dominance in the ensuing sequence.
theory_units.applies_when: You want to shift focus and emphasize the importance of specific characters, especially leaders, in a negotiation or interaction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws audience attention to the characters' expressions and reactions, conveying their authority and emotional state, making them central to the narrative.

theory_units.title: Accelerated Pacing Post-Resolution
theory_units.summary: After a significant event or resolution, accelerate the pacing of character movements to avoid an anticlimactic feeling.
theory_units.applies_when: Characters are moving away from a resolved event or conference, and you want to maintain narrative momentum.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents an anticlimactic drop in energy, maintains audience engagement, and conveys the changed urgency or resolution.

theory_units.title: Inverse Movement Composition
theory_units.summary: To depict characters moving away from each other, reverse the camera and editing formulas used for characters moving towards each other.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing characters who are separating or increasing distance, mirroring a previously established 'moving towards' technique.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a clear visual representation of separation, maintaining a consistent stylistic approach to movement, and conveying a sense of finality or increasing distance.

theory_units.title: Right Angle for Divergent Paths
theory_units.summary: Use right-angle camera coverage to clearly register characters moving away from each other on divergent paths.
theory_units.applies_when: Characters are moving away from each other on paths that diverge, and you want to emphasize their increasing separation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually emphasizes the separation and the growing distance between characters, making their divergent paths clear to the audience.

theory_units.title: Parting Curtain Reveal
theory_units.summary: Use a crowd parting from the center to the sides across a series of progressively tighter shots to reveal a hidden goal or stationary characters behind them.
theory_units.applies_when: A group of characters is obscuring a key element or other characters, and you want to dramatically reveal what is behind them.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a sense of anticipation and spectacle, guiding the audience's eye to the revealed subject, akin to a theatrical curtain opening.

theory_units.title: Movement-Obscured Jump Cut
theory_units.summary: To cut between two static shots of the same subject without a visual jump, introduce a passer-by whose movement temporarily obscures the subject, cutting during this obstruction.
theory_units.applies_when: You need to cut between two different shot sizes of a static subject (e.g., Long Shot to Medium Shot) and avoid a jarring jump cut.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a seamless transition despite the static subject, misdirecting the audience's eye with the passer-by's movement, and smoothly changing the shot size.
theory_units.caution: The distracting movement must feel natural within the scene to avoid drawing undue attention to the edit itself.

theory_units.title: Smooth Cut via Foreground Mask (General Principle)
theory_units.summary: A smooth cut is achieved by having a moving foreground element briefly obscure a stationary subject at the cut point, often leading to a closer view.
theory_units.applies_when: When transitioning between shots, particularly changing shot size or angle of a stationary subject, to ensure visual continuity and hide the cut.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a seamless passage from one shot to the next, hiding the actual cut, and can subtly redirect audience attention.
theory_units.caution: The moving figure doesn't need to completely fill the screen, but should hide the person to be shown in closer view.

theory_units.title: Smooth Cut via Foreground Mask (Existing Player)
theory_units.summary: An already present (possibly static) foreground player moves across the frame to obscure a stationary background player, facilitating a smooth cut.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character is already on screen and can be utilized to create a seamless transition to another character or shot, especially a closer view.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a smooth visual transition, often leading to a closer view or a shift in focus without a jarring cut.

theory_units.title: Smooth Cut via Foreground Mask (Reverse Reveal)
theory_units.summary: Transitioning from a close shot of a static performer to a wider shot by introducing a foreground player who moves to disclose the static performer in the background.
theory_units.applies_when: When moving back from a close shot of a static performer to a wider view, especially when motion is desired to be sharply introduced at the beginning of the second shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a smooth transition from close to wide, dramatically revealing the scene context and reintroducing motion.
theory_units.caution: Background movement can be introduced behind the static player and continue during the second shot without interfering, as closer movement is sharper and dominant.

theory_units.title: Smooth Cut via Foreground Mask (Important Player Reintroduction)
theory_units.summary: An important character's movement is used to facilitate a smooth cut, obscuring and then revealing another character, while simultaneously reintroducing the important character to the audience and clarifying spatial relationships.
theory_units.applies_when: Reintroducing an important character while smoothly transitioning between shots of a static player, and clarifying their position relative to another character in the frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Achieves a smooth cut, dramatically reintroduces a character, and visually clarifies spatial relationships for the audience.

theory_units.title: Smooth Cut via Background Mask (Emphasizing Mover)
theory_units.summary: A cut is made when a moving player passes *behind* a static foreground subject, with the moving player then emerging from behind the static subject in the second shot, shifting emphasis to the mover.
theory_units.applies_when: When desiring to emphasize a character who is moving behind a static subject, making the moving character more important.
theory_units.expected_effect: Shifts the audience's attention and emphasis to the moving player, creating a dynamic transition.
theory_units.caution: The static subject must be in the center of the screen in the first take to get an effective cut from shot to shot.

theory_units.title: Smooth Cut with Right Angle Camera Sites (Moving Subject)
theory_units.summary: A smooth cut is achieved between a shot featuring a moving subject and a static shot by using a static foreground subject to momentarily block the moving subject. The camera positions for the two shots are at a right angle.
theory_units.applies_when: Linking a shot involving a moving subject (e.g., panning shot) with a static shot, particularly when changing camera position significantly (e.g., to a right angle).
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides smooth continuity despite a significant camera angle change, creates dynamic visual emphasis for the motion, and can introduce a character's reaction.
theory_units.caution: The movement recorded in the first shot can last longer than that in the second where the subject moves out of shot quickly due to its increase in size, thus creating a dynamic visual emphasis for the motion itself.

theory_units.title: Smooth Cut with Right Angle Camera Sites (Subordinate Link)
theory_units.summary: Two static main players, featured separately in shots taken from right-angle camera positions, are linked by the movement and departure of a subordinate subject.
theory_units.applies_when: When introducing a second static main player dramatically, relating two static players without an explicit establishing shot, or when opposed glances would be detrimental to the scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a more dramatic and clear introduction of the second player, establishes spatial relationships without direct confrontation, and allows main players to have individual centers of interest.
theory_units.caution: This method disposes of the need for an establishing shot where both main players (A and B) would be shown together, giving the audience their true physical positions on the set.

theory_units.title: Smooth Cut (Both Players Moving, Crossing)
theory_units.summary: When two players are in motion and cross each other in the center of the screen, the cut is made at the point where one player temporarily hides the other. Both shots are typically taken on the same visual axis.
theory_units.applies_when: When transitioning between shots where both main characters are moving and their paths intersect, especially when on a common visual axis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures a smooth cut between moving subjects, maintaining visual continuity and flow.

theory_units.title: Smooth Cut via Foreground Distraction (Receding Subject)
theory_units.summary: To achieve a smooth cut to a closer shot of a subject receding in a neutral direction (which would normally cause a jarring size change), a strong foreground movement is introduced to temporarily block the receding subject at the cut point.
theory_units.applies_when: Cutting forward on the same visual axis to a subject moving away from the camera, which would otherwise result in a visually jarring size change (diminishing then suddenly increasing).
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures a smooth cut, prevents jarring visual effects from sudden size changes, and redirects audience attention.
theory_units.caution: Cutting directly to a closer shot on the same visual axis of a subject moving in a neutral direction is visually jarring because the figure recedes and diminishes in size, then would suddenly increase again.

theory_units.title: Smooth Cut (Crowd Scenes, Distracting Movement)
theory_units.summary: In scenes with an abundance of conflicting movements (e.g., disorganized crowds), a distracting foreground movement is used to smooth the cut and hide potential mismatches.
theory_units.applies_when: Editing shots within busy crowd scenes where multiple, opposed movements make precise matching difficult and could lead to noticeable visual jumps, especially when on the same visual axis or when changing shot size.
theory_units.expected_effect: Achieves a smooth cut in chaotic environments, making mismatches in background movement go unnoticed, and maintaining visual fluidity.
theory_units.caution: Abundance of movement, especially conflicting motion in disorganized crowds, presents difficulties for a precisely matched cut, often leading to very noticeable visual jumps.

theory_units.title: Smooth Cut with Right Angle (Dual Foreground Mask, Crowd)
theory_units.summary: To cut to a closer, side view of a stationary subject within a busy crowd, a right-angle camera change is combined with two foreground persons successively masking the subject.
theory_units.applies_when: Cutting to a closer view of a subject in a crowd, especially when changing camera position significantly (e.g., to a right angle) and a dynamic foreground mask is needed to manage the busy background.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a smooth cut, emphasizes the main subject despite a busy background, and effectively changes the audience's perspective.

theory_units.title: Smooth Cut (Time Transition, Role Reversal)
theory_units.summary: A moving foreground player hides a stationary main subject. A cut occurs on the same visual axis, and in the second shot, a new foreground figure moves away to disclose a different (or same, but transposed) static character in close shot, suggesting a change in time.
theory_units.applies_when: When desiring a strong visual transition that also implies a passage of time or a significant shift in character presence, often used to create a startling effect.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a startling effect, smoothly transitions between scenes, and effectively conveys a change in time.

theory_units.title: Smooth Cut (Redirecting Attention on Receding Subject)
theory_units.summary: When cutting back from a close shot to a long shot of a person moving in a neutral direction, a dominant foreground action is introduced at the beginning of the second shot to redirect audience attention to the main performer.
theory_units.applies_when: Cutting back from a close shot to a long shot of a person moving away, where the main subject's movement might otherwise appear minimized and weakened due to distance.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures a smooth cut, compensates for the weakened movement of the main subject in a long shot, and effectively maintains audience focus on the central performer.
theory_units.caution: When cutting back from a close shot to a long shot of a person moving in a neutral direction, the problem of size is very acute in the second shot, because the distance involved minimizes and weakens movement.

theory_units.title: Foreground Distraction for Background Mismatches (Crowd)
theory_units.summary: Introduce a subordinate player with strong foreground motion at the beginning of a shot to redirect audience attention and mask continuity mismatches in the background, especially in crowd scenes.
theory_units.applies_when: When cutting between shots in a crowd scene where background elements might mismatch, or when needing to smoothly transition between perspectives while obscuring minor inconsistencies.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience attention is drawn to the foreground, making them less likely to notice continuity errors in the background. Creates a smooth visual transition.

theory_units.title: Foreground Player Blocks Camera Lens
theory_units.summary: Block the camera lens entirely with a foreground player's strong, crossing movement at the beginning of the second shot to mask continuity mismatches of a main player advancing or performing a crucial action.
theory_units.applies_when: When a cut might reveal a mismatch in a main player's movement or position from the previous shot, especially if the screen direction needs to be 'reset' or if a player's movement isn't perfectly matched.
theory_units.expected_effect: The strong foreground motion and temporary obscuring of the frame hides the precise start of the main player's action, allowing for greater flexibility in continuity.

theory_units.title: Non-Human Elements Block Lens Transition
theory_units.summary: Use natural phenomena (water, sand, dust, smoke) or light effects (flash, flare, shadow) to momentarily block or obscure the camera lens, serving as a transition point and masking device to reveal a new shot, angle, or closer view.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing a visually distinct and naturalistic transition between shots, especially to hide cuts or emphasize a reveal without using human blocking.
theory_units.expected_effect: A dynamic and often atmospheric transition, guiding audience focus and potentially masking continuity errors or changes in scene setup.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the effect is integrated naturally into the scene to avoid feeling forced or distracting.

theory_units.title: Parting Curtain Effect for Faked Stunts
theory_units.summary: To hide a faked dangerous stunt when cutting on action is not possible, introduce a foreground motion that begins centrally and parts to the sides (like curtains) at the beginning of the second shot, obscuring the critical moment of the stunt.
theory_units.applies_when: When a dangerous stunt must be faked, and the director cannot cut directly on the action due to safety or practical limitations.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience perceives the full action of the stunt without seeing the dangerous part, maintaining realism and safety. The parting motion naturally reveals the aftermath.
theory_units.caution: The foreground distraction must be convincing and relevant to the scene to avoid drawing undue attention to the faking.

theory_units.title: Circular Movement - Tangential External Cameras
theory_units.summary: To clearly cover a performer's circular movement, use two back-to-back reverse camera positions placed tangentially outside the circle, breaking the motion across half-screen areas in each shot. A third camera can be placed inside the circle.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character performs a distinct circular movement and the director wants to emphasize the circularity and potentially link locations or maintain clear screen direction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually clear depiction of circular motion, maintaining consistent screen direction and potentially creating a seamless transition between different locations.
theory_units.caution: Ensure screen direction changes by reason of the circular path are clearly visible.

theory_units.title: Circular Movement - Internal Camera Coverage
theory_units.summary: Cover a performer's circular movement using back-to-back reverse camera positions placed *inside* the circular path, using off-screen glances or anticipation to stress the circular nature of the path.
theory_units.applies_when: When the narrative benefits from a more immersive or internal perspective of a circular movement, perhaps to keep the background stable or emphasize the actor's experience.
theory_units.expected_effect: A dynamic portrayal of circular motion that can feel more intimate or focused on the performer, with the circularity subtly reinforced by the performer's actions.

theory_units.title: Circular Movement - Mixed Internal/External Cameras
theory_units.summary: Combine one camera position outside the circular path and another inside it to cover a circular movement. This will reverse the player's screen position from shot to shot, but their direction of movement on screen should remain consistent to maintain clarity.
theory_units.applies_when: When desiring a shift in perspective on a circular movement, combining external observation with a more involved internal view.
theory_units.expected_effect: A varied and dynamic visual representation of circular movement, with players transposed across the screen but maintaining a clear sense of direction.
theory_units.caution: Carefully manage the screen direction to avoid disorientation despite the transposition of players.

theory_units.title: Circular Movement - Two Performers, Converging Tangential External
theory_units.summary: Use tangential external reverse camera positions to cover a circular movement where one performer approaches a static one. This transposes their screen positions, with both performers' movements converging towards the center of the screen.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting one character moving in a circular path towards another stationary character, emphasizing their interaction and the journey.
theory_units.expected_effect: A dynamic and purposeful approach, visually connecting the moving and static characters as they converge towards the screen's center.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the 'implied' center of interest is clear when only one player is visible.

theory_units.title: Circular Movement - Around Group, Same-Side Re-entry
theory_units.summary: When covering a player's circular movement around a static group, use one internal and one external reverse camera position. Have the moving player exit the frame on one side and then re-enter the *same* side in the subsequent shot to clearly clarify the circular path.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character circles a group of static individuals, and it's important to clearly communicate the continuous circular motion to the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Reinforces the circular nature of the movement, especially useful when the player is off-screen for a period, making their reappearance intuitive.

theory_units.title: Circular Movement - Background to Foreground with Pause
theory_units.summary: To depict a circular movement transitioning from background to foreground using external reverse camera angles, include a pause at the end of the first shot to account for the off-screen travel time of the moving player before their re-entry in the foreground of the second shot.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character completes a portion of a circular path off-screen between two shots, moving from a background to a foreground position.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents the audience from feeling disoriented or confused by the sudden appearance of the character, providing a natural pace for the implied off-screen journey.
theory_units.caution: The pause length should be judicious, long enough to justify travel but not so long as to drag the scene.

theory_units.title: Circular Movement - Right Angle Emphasis on Static Player
theory_units.summary: To emphasize a static player while another performs a circular movement behind them, use a right-angle camera placement. Cover the main circular motion with a panning shot in the first shot, then cut to a close-up of the static player in the second, with the moving player briefly exiting from behind them.
theory_units.applies_when: When the focus needs to shift or settle on a static character after a dynamic circular movement by another, using the movement to transition to the emphasis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws audience attention to the static player, highlighting their reaction or significance after the preceding movement, maximizing screen activity.

theory_units.title: Circular Movement - Justified Same-Shot Opposite Side Re-entry
theory_units.summary: To allow a player to exit one side of the screen and re-enter from the opposite side within the *same shot* (implying off-screen circular motion), justify the movement for the audience through a static player's head turn, a mirror reflection, or a combination of mirror and camera zoom.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to show a player completing a circular path off-screen and re-entering the frame from the opposite side without cutting, and without disorienting the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains a continuous shot while creating the illusion of a complete circular movement, preventing audience confusion about the player's whereabouts.
theory_units.caution: If using a mirror, careful blocking is required to conceal the camera. The justification (head turn/mirror) must be convincing and naturally integrated.

theory_units.title: Strong Vertical Entrance (Same Visual Axis)
theory_units.summary: To strongly punctuate an upward vertical motion, cut from a wider shot where a subject moves out of frame upwards to a closer shot where they rise into the frame, maintaining a common visual axis.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character performs a significant upward vertical movement and the director wants to emphasize or clearly punctuate this motion, making their entrance notable.
theory_units.expected_effect: A strong and clear punctuation of the performed vertical motion, making the subject's entrance into the frame feel deliberate and impactful.
theory_units.caution: This effect can also be achieved without the player completely moving out of the first shot (if seen in a long shot), by solely relying on the entrance motion in the closer second shot.

theory_units.title: Right Angle Coverage for Upward Vertical Movement
theory_units.summary: Cover an upward vertical movement by first showing the subject rising in a side-view shot, then cutting to a frontal shot where they enter from below, with the second camera position being higher.
theory_units.applies_when: When capturing a subject's upward vertical movement and seeking to accompany their rise with a dynamic change in camera perspective.
theory_units.expected_effect: Effectively accompanies the upward movement of the rising player, providing a clear progression in their ascent.

theory_units.title: Reverse Angle Coverage for Vertical Movement (Pivot)
theory_units.summary: Utilize reverse (external) camera angles for vertical movement, particularly when the rising player can be used as a pivot in the scene, with the second camera position higher to follow their ascent.
theory_units.applies_when: When a vertical movement is central to the scene and the rising player acts as a pivotal point, allowing for external angle coverage.
theory_units.expected_effect: Accompanies the upward movement of the rising player while leveraging their position as a scene pivot, potentially offering new visual information from the reverse angle.

theory_units.title: Transforming Horizontal to Vertical with High Camera Angle
theory_units.summary: A horizontal movement can be perceived as vertical on screen in a subsequent shot by placing the camera high and pointing downwards.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to create the illusion of vertical motion on screen from an originally horizontal movement, or to provide a different perspective on character travel.
theory_units.expected_effect: Transforms the audience's perception of horizontal movement into a vertical ascent or descent on screen.
theory_units.caution: If the camera follows with a vertical upward tilt in the second shot, players will remain in the same screen sector until the tilt stops, then they will ascend the screen.

theory_units.title: Mirror Editing for Downward Motion
theory_units.summary: Edit a downward motion by first showing the action reflected in a mirror, then cutting to the real action, with both occurring in the same picture sector.
theory_units.applies_when: When seeking an imaginative or curious way to introduce or emphasize a downward motion, using a reflective surface.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a curious and unique editing effect, where the reflected and real vertical actions are visually linked and occur in the same screen area, providing a novel approach to a common event.

theory_units.title: Right Angle Arc Movement to Reveal
theory_units.summary: When a subject performs an arc-like movement (e.g., sitting down), use a right-angle camera position to have the foreground subject block the screen and then reveal another subject beyond.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character's body moves through an arc (like sitting) and the director wishes to create an interesting effect or reveal another character through that movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: An interesting visual effect and a dramatic reveal of a companion previously obscured by the foreground player's movement.

theory_units.title: Vertical Object Lowering with Screen Repetition & Detail
theory_units.summary: Present a vertical object lowering in two shots, where the first brings the object to the picture's center and the second (a closer shot on the same visual axis) shows details as the object enters from above and is lowered.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character is lowering an object and the director wants to show the action while also emphasizing the object's details.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearly presents the vertical lowering motion while drawing attention to the details of the object, potentially using the upper screen area for both shots for continuity.
theory_units.caution: A reverse angle can be used for the second shot to contrast arc paths while maintaining the vertical direction.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Stop: Abrupt Halt (Common Visual Axis)
theory_units.summary: To create a dynamic stop, present an actor moving at full speed in the first shot and then abruptly stopping after only a couple of steps forward in the second shot, utilizing a common visual axis for both cameras.
theory_units.applies_when: When an actor's movement (especially running) is intended to end abruptly, and the director wants to stress the violence or force of the halt.
theory_units.expected_effect: The stop comes as a slight shock, powerfully stressing the abruptness and force of the halt, as the preceding shot implied continuous motion.
theory_units.caution: The effect is stronger if the player jumps down an obstacle (trench, pit, stairs) that is suddenly revealed by moving the second camera backward.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Stop: Rolling to Rest (Compensating Axis)
theory_units.summary: Apply the dynamic stop technique to rolling action, showing performers rolling almost out of view in the first shot, then coming to rest in the center of the picture area in a second shot, from a camera behind the first but on the same visual axis.
theory_units.applies_when: When capturing a struggle or rolling action where performers come to a sudden rest, and the director wishes to emphasize the dramatic impact of this halt.
theory_units.expected_effect: Dramatically enhances the action, bringing the performers to a central, emphasized halt. The second shot compensates for the inadequate coverage of the first, re-centering the action.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Stop: Overhead to Level View
theory_units.summary: Combine an overhead shot with a level camera position in the second shot to achieve a dynamic stop, bringing a walking or running player to a halt after a few steps.
theory_units.applies_when: When a player (or group) is moving and needs to come to an abrupt halt, and the director wants to use contrasting camera angles to enhance the effect.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a dynamic stop by shifting perspective, emphasizing the halt. The number of steps needed before stopping (1 for walking, 2-3 for running) adjusts the impact.
theory_units.caution: Works for both single individuals and groups moving in the same direction.

theory_units.title: Justification for Camera Movement
theory_units.summary: All camera movement must be justified, contributing to clearer, more dynamic, and precise storytelling.
theory_units.applies_when: Before deciding to use any form of camera movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clearer, more dynamic, and precise storytelling.
theory_units.caution: Unjudicious use of a moving camera can easily destroy illusion, become an annoyance, and conflict with the pace and meaning of the story.

theory_units.title: POV for Heightened Physical Sensation
theory_units.summary: Use a moving camera from a character's point of view to give the audience a heightened physical sensation, especially when the character is involved in violent motion.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character experiences a violent or intense physical sensation (e.g., loss of control, fear) and the director wants the audience to share that feeling directly.
theory_units.expected_effect: The audience experiences a heightened physical sensation, mirroring the character's internal state, leading to greater involvement and empathy.
theory_units.caution: Often used momentarily, cutting back to exterior shots to avoid audience awareness of a 'trick'.

theory_units.title: Subjective Camera: Camera as Actor
theory_units.summary: Employ the 'subjective technique' where the camera behaves as if it is an actor's eyes, lurching, staggering, or moving like a performer, with other actors reacting directly into the lens.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming for profound audience involvement with a character's feelings over an extended period within a shot or sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a deep sense of involvement with the character's feeling, as the audience literally occupies their perspective and is treated as an active participant by other performers.
theory_units.caution: This technique is difficult to pull off successfully because the audience is often aware of the 'trick' being played on them, potentially breaking immersion if not carefully executed. Full-length features using this technique have revealed its limitations.

theory_units.title: Panning/Tracking for Information Disclosure (Direct vs. Subjective)
theory_units.summary: Panning or tracking shots can present information directly (documentary style, no character context) or subjectively (character's view, with preceding/following shots showing the character watching).
theory_units.applies_when: When the director needs to convey visual information, either as objective fact or through the specific viewpoint of a character.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides information to the audience, either impartially or imbued with the emotional context of a character's perspective, fostering greater involvement in the latter case.

theory_units.title: Panning/Tracking for Revelation (Expected or Unexpected)
theory_units.summary: Use panning or tracking shots to gradually disclose an expected or unexpected situation at the end of the camera movement.
theory_units.applies_when: When building suspense towards a predictable outcome, or when aiming to deliver a shocking or humorous surprise to the audience.
theory_units.expected_effect: For expected outcomes: builds anticipation and confirms suspicions. For unexpected outcomes: delivers a strong surprise, challenging audience expectations.
theory_units.caution: The choice between expected and unexpected outcome dictates the final reveal.

theory_units.title: Efficiency of Cutting vs. Moving Shot
theory_units.summary: A straight cut establishes a new point of interest faster than a moving shot, which can expend useless footage if not justified by significant action or objects.
theory_units.applies_when: When deciding whether to cut or pan/track to a new point of interest, considering pace and narrative efficiency.
theory_units.expected_effect: A straight cut results in a faster establishment of a new point. An unjustified moving shot can cause the sequence to drag and waste footage.
theory_units.caution: Significant action or objects must be photographed during a pan or track to justify its use; otherwise, the sequence may drag.

theory_units.title: Pan/Track with Secondary Subject to Primary Focus
theory_units.summary: Pan or track with a secondary subject that enters and then leaves the frame, using their movement to guide the camera towards and ultimately stop on a new, primary center of interest.
theory_units.applies_when: When transitioning focus from a general scene to specific characters or objects, using a less important moving subject as a visual 'guide'.
theory_units.expected_effect: Smoothly shifts audience attention from one area or group to a new, specific center of interest, often introducing main characters organically.

theory_units.title: Structure and Cutting of Pan/Track Shots
theory_units.summary: A panning or tracking shot typically has three parts: a static beginning, a moving middle, and a static conclusion. A cut from a moving shot to a static shot of the same static subject will cause a visual jump, but cutting after the camera has come to a standstill is permissible.
theory_units.applies_when: When planning the composition and editing of shots involving camera movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains visual continuity and avoids jarring jump cuts if cutting rules are followed.
theory_units.caution: Cannot cut from a moving to a static shot of the same static person or object as a visual jump would occur. Only cut after the camera has come to a standstill.

theory_units.title: Combined Panning and Tracking for Complex Follows
theory_units.summary: Combine panning and tracking movements to smoothly follow a subject or vehicle, especially when it changes direction or enters new spaces.
theory_units.applies_when: When a subject's movement involves changes in direction or requires the camera to transition between following and revealing new environments.
theory_units.expected_effect: Seamlessly follows complex subject movement, maintaining focus and providing a smooth visual experience as the scene unfolds.

theory_units.title: Editing Repetitive Action Tracking Shots
theory_units.summary: Tracking shots of repetitive action can be cut to any desired length, broken into fragments, and intercut with other shots in editing.
theory_units.applies_when: When filming subjects performing continuous or repetitive actions (e.g., a car moving, a person walking) and requiring flexibility in editing duration or sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides significant editing flexibility, allowing the director to adjust scene pacing, create parallel action, or break up sequences as needed.

theory_units.title: Continuity of Screen Sector and Direction (Moving-to-Static Cuts)
theory_units.summary: When cutting from a pan or track to a static shot showing a moving person or object, maintain the subject framed in the same screen sector and ensure constant screen direction.
theory_units.applies_when: When transitioning from a moving camera shot to a static camera shot that features a continuously moving subject.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures visual continuity and smoother cuts, preventing jarring disorientation for the audience by maintaining consistent spatial and directional cues.

theory_units.title: Selective Inclusion/Exclusion with Camera Motion
theory_units.summary: Use panning or tracking to selectively exclude undesired material and introduce new persons, objects, or backgrounds into the scene while moving with a central action.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director needs to control what the audience sees within a moving shot, guiding their attention and revealing new elements as the central action progresses.
theory_units.expected_effect: Efficiently manages the on-screen information, drawing focus to the central action while seamlessly incorporating or removing elements from the frame.

theory_units.title: Precision in Panning/Tracking Execution
theory_units.summary: Execute panning or tracking shots in a secure, precise, and decisive manner, avoiding jerky, indecisive, or amateurish movements.
theory_units.applies_when: During the execution of any panning or tracking shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Achieves a professional and polished visual aesthetic, ensuring smooth and intentional camera work.
theory_units.caution: Jerky panning or indecisive pivoting reveals an amateur, inexperienced conception and execution, detracting from the film's quality.

theory_units.title: Subject Leads Camera Movement
theory_units.summary: Allow the subject to initiate movement before the camera follows, and stop the camera's motion before the subject completely stops to allow them to move slightly further on screen.
theory_units.applies_when: When following a moving subject with the camera, aiming for a natural and unobtrusive camera movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Makes the subject's movement the primary focus, subtly guiding the audience's eye, and creates a more natural flow, reducing the perception of the camera's own motion.

theory_units.title: Simple Camera Paths for Complex Subject Action
theory_units.summary: For continuous pans or tracks, move the camera along simple paths and allow the actors or vehicles to perform all the complicated motions within the frame area.
theory_units.applies_when: When a scene features intricate or complex subject movement that needs to be captured by a moving camera.
theory_units.expected_effect: Simplifies camera operation while highlighting the dynamism and complexity of the subject's actions, keeping the focus on the performers/vehicles.

theory_units.title: Balanced Composition for Pan/Track Start/End
theory_units.summary: Panning or tracking shots should begin and conclude with pictorially balanced visual compositions.
theory_units.applies_when: When initiating and concluding any panning or tracking shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures that the shot feels aesthetically complete and stable at its start and end points, providing visual harmony.

theory_units.title: Appropriate Timing for Panning/Tracking Shots
theory_units.summary: The duration of camera motion in a panning or tracking shot must be precisely timed; too short or too long a movement will detract from the story.
theory_units.applies_when: When determining the length and pacing of moving camera shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Supports the narrative effectively and maintains appropriate scene pacing.
theory_units.caution: Too short or too long a movement will work against the story being told, either by rushing or dragging the audience's experience.

theory_units.title: Small Camera Moves for Re-establishing Balance
