theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to maintain a continuous, overall movement (e.g., tracking through a battle) while simultaneously drawing attention to individual characters or details at specific moments.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains scene flow while allowing for selective emphasis, creating a dynamic and immersive experience that highlights both the broad action and key individual elements.

theory_units.title: Masking Zooms with Track and Pan
theory_units.summary: Combining tracking and panning with a zoom can mask the zoom motion, creating an illusion of unhampered camera movement and rendering the zoom almost imperceptible if executed slowly.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to incorporate a zoom effect without it being overtly noticeable or artificial, aiming for a fluid and natural camera flow.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a seamless and organic camera movement, allowing the zoom to serve its purpose (e.g., re-framing, emphasizing) without drawing attention to itself.
theory_units.caution: The zoom must be slow enough to be rendered almost imperceptible when combined with tracking and panning.

theory_units.title: Opposed Track and Zoom Distortion
theory_units.summary: Combining a camera tracking backward with a simultaneous lens zoom forward creates a peculiar optical distortion of distances and object sizes.
theory_units.applies_when: To achieve a startling visual effect, especially in enclosed spaces like corridors, conveying disorientation or a strange perception of depth and size.
theory_units.expected_effect: Peculiar distortion of distances and object sizes, a 'startling visual effect', sense of disorientation.

theory_units.title: Three-Quarter Angle Track Back & Oblique Zoom
theory_units.summary: A camera angled three-quarters to a group, moving backward at full speed, then zooming in obliquely towards the subjects, creates a subtle visual distortion and dynamic movement.
theory_units.applies_when: To create a dynamic and subtly distorting shot when moving in front of a group, such as a cavalry charge, without being as 'blunt' as a full opposed track/zoom.
theory_units.expected_effect: Subtle visual distortion, dynamic movement, immersive feeling with the group.

theory_units.title: Zooming Through Foreground Obstacles
theory_units.summary: Start a zoom shot on wide angle with foreground and background in focus; as the lens moves to telephoto, foreground objects blur into color, revealing the sharply focused main action.
theory_units.applies_when: To dramatically reveal main action or a character by initially obscuring them behind foreground obstacles, creating a sense of discovery.
theory_units.expected_effect: Dramatic revelation of main action, increased visual interest, selective focus, sense of looking through something.

theory_units.title: Animated Foreground Obstacles for Zoom
theory_units.summary: Enhances the effect of zooming through foreground obstacles if the irregular foreground objects themselves have movement, preferably a repetitive motion.
theory_units.applies_when: When utilizing foreground obstacles in a zoom shot, to add an extra layer of dynamism and visual texture to the revelation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased visual interest and dynamism, more complex visual texture, heightened sense of movement in the scene.

theory_units.title: Vehicle Overturn Camera Trick
theory_units.summary: Simulate a vehicle overturning by filming it speeding diagonally towards the camera, panning to follow until it fills the frame, then suddenly rotating the camera on its side.
theory_units.applies_when: To create the visual effect of a vehicle overturning spectacularly without actual destruction, often for high-speed crash sequences.
theory_units.expected_effect: Illusion of a vehicle overturning, heightened drama, intense action.
theory_units.caution: The horizon line must not be visible on screen, and the camera must be tilted in a direction contrary to the moving vehicle.

theory_units.title: Show, Don't Tell in Action Scenes
theory_units.summary: Prioritize visual storytelling over dialogue in action scenes to maintain momentum and clarify events, with dialogue reduced to brief commands or used as strategic pauses.
theory_units.applies_when: During action sequences to maximize visual impact, maintain audience engagement, and ensure the narrative is conveyed through direct observation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Heightened action, clearer visual narrative, sustained tension and pace.
theory_units.caution: Continuous action can saturate emotion; dialogue can be used in pauses to clarify story points or give audience rest.

theory_units.title: Pacing Action with Pauses
theory_units.summary: Introduce strategic pauses within continuous action sequences to prevent audience emotional saturation, allowing for renewed interest and clarity, potentially using verbal explanations during these breaks.
theory_units.applies_when: During extended action sequences to manage audience emotion, prevent fatigue, and provide narrative clarification or character respite.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintained audience engagement, prevention of emotional fatigue, clearer understanding of story points, renewed tension after the pause.
theory_units.caution: Pauses should be purposeful and contribute to the rhythm of the action scene.

theory_units.title: Combat Sequence Pacing: Slow Build, Quick Resolve
theory_units.summary: Effectively structure combat by building tension slowly, often including a physical pause for combatants to recuperate, then resolving the fight quickly with a brief, decisive exchange of blows.
theory_units.applies_when: When designing a physical combat sequence to control tension, build anticipation, and deliver a satisfying, impactful resolution.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased tension, dramatic climax, audience anticipation and emotional investment.

theory_units.title: Visual Introduction of Tools (Mechanism Defiance)
theory_units.summary: When depicting characters overcoming a mechanism, visually present the tools they will use, but provide no or only partial explanations of their intended employment to build suspense.
theory_units.applies_when: In sequences where characters confront and attempt to conquer a dangerous mechanism, to create anticipation and demonstrate ingenuity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased suspense, audience engagement through implied ingenuity, anticipation of how tools will be used.
theory_units.caution: Avoid full explanations to maintain mystery and allow for visual discovery during the action.

theory_units.title: Unpredictable Chase Outcome through Obstacles
theory_units.summary: Maintain audience unpredictability in chase outcomes by visually presenting a diverse range of obstacles for both pursuers and hunted, keeping the resolution uncertain.
theory_units.applies_when: When staging a chase sequence to maximize audience engagement and prevent the outcome from being easily foreseen.
theory_units.expected_effect: Sustained audience suspense, dynamic visual variety, unpredictable narrative progression.

theory_units.title: Location Design for Complex Chases
theory_units.summary: Choose intricate buildings and environments for complex chase variations (e.g., double chase) as they offer visual obstacles and possibilities, while open ground nullifies their effect.
theory_units.applies_when: When scouting or designing locations for chase sequences that involve multiple parties, varied paths, or intricate maneuvering.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhanced complexity and visual interest in chase scenes, increased tension through environmental obstacles.
theory_units.caution: Open ground diminishes the effectiveness of complex chase variations like the double chase.

theory_units.title: Pacing Action Resolution
theory_units.summary: Action sequences should conclude promptly after their narrative resolution; a humorous scene can then be used to effectively release built-up tension.
theory_units.applies_when: After the climax or resolution of an action sequence, to ensure efficient storytelling and manage the audience's emotional state.
theory_units.expected_effect: Satisfying and concise conclusion to action, effective emotional release for the audience, smooth transition to subsequent scenes.
theory_units.caution: Do not extend the action beyond its resolution point for too long, as this can diminish impact.

theory_units.title: Impersonal Point of View
theory_units.summary: The camera observes events externally, examining all players and situations without adopting any single character's perspective, thus positioning the audience as a detached spectator.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants the audience to observe action objectively, without strong emotional identification with a specific character, for a broader understanding of events.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience detachment, objective observation of events, broad understanding of the scene without deep emotional immersion.
theory_units.caution: This approach deliberately limits emotional participation from the audience towards individual characters.

theory_units.title: Subjective Point of View (Passive Observer)
theory_units.summary: To present action from a central player's passive viewpoint, use frontal close-up reaction shots of the character, intercut with long shots showing the action they are watching from their exact position.
theory_units.applies_when: When a central character is passively witnessing an event, to immerse the audience emotionally through their perspective and reactions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Strong audience identification with the character, emotional participation, heightened empathy and suspense through their gaze.

theory_units.title: Subjective Point of View (Active Participant - Setup)
theory_units.summary: When a player is actively engaged in action, establish the scene by emphasizing the central player with frontal close shots and close-ups, while showing distant views of their opponent.
theory_units.applies_when: During the setup phase of active combat or confrontation, to maintain emphasis on the protagonist's perspective and emotional involvement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Strong audience identification with the central character, heightened sense of their immediate involvement and the challenge they face.
theory_units.caution: This phase focuses on the protagonist's view, keeping the opponent somewhat distant.

theory_units.title: Combat POV Transition: Impersonal to Subjective
theory_units.summary: During physical combat, use full shots (impersonal POV) to clearly cover both combatants, then revert to the central character's subjective close-up POV as they separate, re-emphasizing the main player.
theory_units.applies_when: During direct physical engagement in action scenes, to balance clarity of the fight with emotional emphasis on the protagonist.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clear presentation of combat, re-establishment of emotional connection and visual emphasis with the protagonist after the direct confrontation.

theory_units.title: Exclusions in Subjective Reaction Shots
theory_units.summary: In subjective point-of-view reaction shots, the central character should not be seen in the foreground, nor from their opponent’s point of view, to maintain the immersive illusion of their perspective.
theory_units.applies_when: When maintaining a consistent subjective point of view for a central character, especially in reaction or observation shots.
theory_units.expected_effect: Sustained audience immersion and identification with the subjective character, preventing a break in the illusion.
theory_units.caution: Violating these exclusions shifts the POV to objective and breaks audience immersion.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Subjective POV During Character Movement
theory_units.summary: If the main player (whose POV the audience shares) moves, preserve the subjective perspective by panning or tracking the camera with them within the same static shot, avoiding cuts to wider, objective shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When the subjective character needs to move within the scene, to preserve emotional immersion and consistency of perspective.
theory_units.expected_effect: Preservation of audience emotion and immersion, continuous subjective experience without breaking the 'fourth wall' of the character's gaze.
theory_units.caution: Cutting to a full or wider shot will break the subjective POV and shift the perspective to objective.

theory_units.title: Alternating Subjective POVs for a Single Event
theory_units.summary: To present a central action from multiple perspectives, show each observer in a close shot, then cut to a long shot depicting the main event from their specific point of view, repeating this pattern for all observers.
theory_units.applies_when: When a significant central action is being observed by multiple characters from different vantage points, to build suspense and provide varied perspectives.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhanced suspense, comprehensive visual coverage of the event from different angles, audience engagement through multiple character perspectives.

theory_units.title: Dominant Central Action Payoff (from Multiple POVs)
theory_units.summary: After establishing a central action through multiple subjective points of view, shift emphasis by moving closer to the main action itself, making it dominant and relating it to its immediate climax or center of interest.
theory_units.applies_when: Following a sequence that uses multiple subjective POVs to observe a central action, to deliver the climax, immediate consequence, or direct engagement of that action.
theory_units.expected_effect: Climactic payoff, heightened intensity, a decisive shift from observation to direct involvement with the central event.

theory_units.title: Emotion-Driven Shifting Subjective POVs
theory_units.summary: Instead of a fixed pattern, subjective points of view shift dynamically, guided by the emotional flow of the event, engaging the audience through varying character perspectives as emotional intensity changes.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering an event with multiple key characters, where the director wants to emphasize the emotional impact on different individuals and guide the audience's emotional journey through shifting perspectives.
theory_units.expected_effect: Stronger emotional engagement, dynamic and fluid storytelling, emphasis on character reactions and internal states.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful management to ensure clarity and avoid audience confusion despite the 'random' shifting.

theory_units.title: Strategic POV Selection for Emotional Arc
theory_units.summary: Within sequences utilizing shifting subjective POVs, strategically choose which character's perspective to use at different moments to achieve specific emotional and narrative effects (e.g., initial observation, wider perspective, intimate involvement).
theory_units.applies_when: When designing a scene with multiple key characters where dynamic emotional engagement and varied perspectives are crucial for the narrative's emotional arc.
theory_units.expected_effect: Guided emotional journey for the audience, enhanced narrative complexity, deeper character insight and empathy.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Camera Mix for Chases (Static & Moving)
theory_units.summary: Enhance chase scenes by alternating static long shots with moving (tracking, hand-held) closer views of subjects, repeating this pattern, with short, sometimes jerky moving shots to add excitement.
theory_units.applies_when: To create visual impact, excitement, and a sense of urgency in chase scenes or sequences of running people.
theory_units.expected_effect: Heightened excitement, visual dynamism, increased audience engagement and immersion in the chase.
theory_units.caution: Moving camera shots should be of short duration (e.g., no more than 5 seconds) to avoid annoying the audience.

theory_units.title: Cumulative Action within a Static Deep-Focus Shot
theory_units.summary: Create excitement by staging multiple, overlapping actions within the various planes of depth of a single static shot, either progressively or simultaneously, from background to foreground.
theory_units.applies_when: To create a complex and exciting action sequence within a single shot, leveraging deep staging and intricate blocking.
theory_units.expected_effect: High visual excitement, a sense of continuous, unfolding action, rich visual information, audience immersion.
theory_units.caution: Actions must overlap swiftly and maintain rhythm to prevent the scene from slackening.

theory_units.title: Two-Shot Split for Emphasizing Blows (or Impacts)
theory_units.summary: To stress the violence of a physical blow or vehicle impact, divide it into two shots: the initial motion in a medium shot, and the concluding impact/swing in a close shot on the same visual axis.
theory_units.applies_when: To heighten the perceived violence, force, and impact of physical blows or collisions in action scenes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased visual impact and perceived violence, visceral audience reaction, dramatic emphasis.
theory_units.caution: Requires shooting two complete takes for editing; maintain a consistent visual axis between the shots.

theory_units.title: Foreground Obstruction for Action Scenes
theory_units.summary: Introduce moving foreground elements (combatants, animals, machines, or static objects filmed with camera movement) between the camera and the main action to create intermittent glimpses, heightening audience interest.
theory_units.applies_when: To add dynamism, suspense, and visual complexity to fighting or action scenes by partially obscuring and revealing the main event.
theory_units.expected_effect: Heightened audience interest and engagement, a sense of chaos or crowdedness, dynamic visual flow, increased intensity.
theory_units.caution: Foreground elements must not linger too long and should exit to be replaced; a long focal lens can be used to throw foreground combatants out of focus.

theory_units.title: Expanding-Contracting Pattern for Battle Coverage
theory_units.summary: In large-scale battles, alternate between wide crowd shots of general action and close-up scenes of hero(es) in personal combat, creating an expanding-contracting pattern that shifts audience focus from general to particular.
theory_units.applies_when: When directing large-scale battle scenes to manage audience perspective, maintain identification with main characters, and convey both spectacle and personal stakes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Stronger audience identification with characters within a larger spectacle, dynamic coverage of the battle, varied emotional engagement, a clearer narrative amidst chaos.
theory_units.caution: Both crowd scenes and protagonist scenes must have a central purpose and not be 'loose' or aimless.

theory_units.title: Climax Pacing: Random Shot Shortening
theory_units.summary: To build tension towards an imminent violent conclusion, use a succession of short shots leading to the payoff, with shot durations randomly decreasing to accelerate the pace.
theory_units.applies_when: When an imminent violent conclusion is anticipated by the audience, to build suspense and accelerate the narrative towards the payoff through abrupt cuts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased urgency, heightened tension, swift and jarring acceleration towards the climax.
theory_units.caution: While 'random', shot lengths should be purposefully shortened to achieve the desired effect.

theory_units.title: Climax Pacing: Progressive Shot Shortening
theory_units.summary: To build tension towards an imminent violent conclusion, use a succession of shots with progressively decreasing durations, culminating rapidly in the climax itself.
theory_units.applies_when: When an imminent violent conclusion is anticipated by the audience, to build suspense and smoothly yet rapidly accelerate the narrative towards the payoff.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased urgency, heightened tension, swift, linear acceleration towards the climax.

theory_units.title: Parallel Editing for Pre-Climax Reactions
theory_units.summary: When building to a disaster or violent conclusion, use parallel editing across multiple narrative lines to showcase various characters' reactions preceding the event, enriching the build-up.
theory_units.applies_when: Leading up to a disaster or violent conclusion, to build suspense and provide a broader emotional context and stakes for the impending event.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased suspense, multi-faceted emotional build-up, broader narrative engagement and understanding of the stakes.

theory_units.title: Progressively Diminishing Shot Length for Climax
theory_units.summary: Reduce the length of individual shots progressively as an event builds towards a visual climax to accelerate tempo and build tension.
theory_units.applies_when: Prior to a visual climax in a sequence, especially when building tension.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a mounting crescendo, quickens the film's tempo, builds brief tension in the audience, which finds relief in the outburst itself.

theory_units.title: Fragmenting Climactic Action with Intercut Reactions
theory_units.summary: Divide expected climactic, exciting, or violent actions into multiple shots and intercut them with character reactions to extend the event and maintain dramatic impact.
theory_units.applies_when: When the audience is expecting a climatic action, especially if the destruction is slow and massive.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a detailed account of the catastrophe, stretches the event in time, doubles the visual pleasure for the audience, maintains dramatic impact, and enriches the version of the event.
theory_units.caution: Presenting the event in its entirety without interruptions lessens its dramatic impact and limits audience pleasure.

theory_units.title: Covering Climaxes with Multiple Points of View
theory_units.summary: Film a single climactic event from several distinct points of view, using each perspective judiciously within the sequence, to provide comprehensive coverage and emotional depth.
theory_units.applies_when: When covering a major catastrophic event or complex climax where multiple facets and emotional impacts are important.
theory_units.expected_effect: Obtains a richer version of the event, extends its on-screen duration by including varied perspectives (e.g., reaction shots), and provides a comprehensive understanding of the catastrophe.
theory_units.caution: Observe that the blowing up of the train was filmed from three points of view. Each of these shots was used only twice in the whole sequence to cover the catastrophe from beginning to conclusion. (Implies judicious use rather than overuse).

theory_units.title: Accelerated Motion (Undercranking)
theory_units.summary: Film at a slower frame rate than normal (e.g., 16 fps or 8 fps) and project at the standard rate (24 fps) to increase the apparent velocity of subjects.
theory_units.applies_when: For chase or action sequences to impart a dynamic effect, or when aiming for a comedic, jerky movement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Imparts a dynamic effect, increases the apparent velocity of the subject, makes movement appear more dramatic. At very low frame rates (e.g., 8 fps), it can produce laughter.
theory_units.caution: Care must be taken not to overdo this effect, or the movement will become so jerky that it will produce laughter (unless laughter is the desired effect).

theory_units.title: Slow Motion (Overcranking)
theory_units.summary: Film at a higher frame rate than normal (e.g., slightly higher than 24 fps) and project at the standard rate (24 fps) to slow down movement on screen.
theory_units.applies_when: To impart majesty to a movement, enhance climactic moments (jumps, plunges, explosions), or for dramatic death scenes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Acquires grace of movement, appears imposing, enhances the scene, adds dramatic weight to climaxes or death scenes.

theory_units.title: Maintaining Sharp Focus (Follow Focus)
theory_units.summary: Continuously adjust the lens focus to keep a subject sharply defined as the camera or subjects move, or as points of interest shift within the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: The camera tracks, pans, or tilts; actors move towards/away from the camera or pass by at different ranges; the camera remains stationary but shifts focus between subjects at different distances.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures the subject remains sharply defined and clear, guiding audience attention effectively.

theory_units.title: Deliberate Selective Focus for Dramatic Effect
theory_units.summary: Intentionally shift focus from one plane of depth (e.g., foreground) to another (e.g., background) within a single shot to create specific dramatic emphasis.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director wants to draw the audience's attention to a different part of the scene, reveal information, or create a specific dramatic effect by changing visual emphasis.
theory_units.expected_effect: Obtains many dramatic effects by selectively highlighting different subjects or areas within the frame.

theory_units.title: Editing in the Camera (Master Shot Choreography)
theory_units.summary: Achieve narrative and dramatic effects within a single, continuous film frame by meticulously choreographing camera and subject movement, eliminating the need for traditional visual cuts.
theory_units.applies_when: When desiring a smoothly flowing scene where the audience is not distracted by cuts, and actors can deliver continuous, uninterrupted performances, similar to theatre.
theory_units.expected_effect: Scene flows smoothly, audience is unaware of the technique, actors have a better chance to drop into their characters, dynamic results, faster shooting speed (if well-executed).
theory_units.caution: Requires careful pre-planning and precise execution; mistakes can be quite expensive, especially for limited budget productions, due to the amount of film expended in retakes. Thorough rehearsals are vital.

theory_units.title: Integrating Physical and In-Camera Editing
theory_units.summary: Combine traditional physical editing (fragmentation) with 'editing within the film frame' techniques to leverage the strengths of both approaches for maximum expressive potential.
theory_units.applies_when: When a filmmaker seeks to overcome the individual limitations of either traditional editing or in-camera editing, and to enrich their expressive screen language.
theory_units.expected_effect: Benefits from the best of both systems, surmounting their individual limitations, resulting in a richer and more versatile expressive screen language.

theory_units.title: Pause Between Movements (In-Camera Editing)
theory_units.summary: Within a continuous 'editing in the camera' shot, introduce deliberate pauses after a player or camera moves to a new zone, holding the position before proceeding to the next.
theory_units.applies_when: When executing a continuous shot where the camera or subjects move through multiple pictorial variations or zones.
theory_units.expected_effect: Allows the audience sufficient time to appreciate and establish each new player or camera position and its pictorial variations.
theory_units.caution: If the movement is continuous and unbroken by pauses, it will become just a following shot, and the audience would not have time to appreciate the pictorial variations.

theory_units.title: Varying Action Zones (In-Camera Editing)
theory_units.summary: Manipulate the arrangement and relationship of action zones within the frame (using stationary, panning, or tracking cameras) to create an impression of space and prevent a static background in continuous shots.
theory_units.applies_when: When using 'editing in the camera' techniques to maintain visual interest and spatial impression in a continuous shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Gives the impression of space wherein the actors move, prevents the background from becoming annoying or monotonous, and enhances visual dynamism.
theory_units.caution: If the camera remains stationary with a constant background, it will constitute a limitation and become annoying in a very short time.

theory_units.title: Approaching or Receding from Camera (Motion in Depth)
theory_units.summary: Utilize motion in depth (moving from foreground to background or vice versa) by subjects within a continuous shot, recorded by a stationary, panning, or tracking camera, to create visual variations and shift attention.
theory_units.applies_when: Desiring dynamic visual changes and clear shifts of action zones within a continuous shot, especially with multiple players.
theory_units.expected_effect: Ensures clear changes of action zones, is easy to execute, simple to understand, and unobtrusive for the audience, who will naturally follow the dominant motion.
theory_units.caution: When a group is involved, it is important that only one player at a time moves from zone to zone, with others remaining in their places.

theory_units.title: Panning to Unite Action Zones
theory_units.summary: A panning camera can seamlessly connect two distinct action zones positioned tangentially to the camera's location, following a player's movement between them.
theory_units.applies_when: When two actors need to be linked through movement within the same shot, or when a player moves between different areas of interest, maintaining visual continuity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates visual unity and continuity across distinct action zones, keeping the moving player as the focus, and can facilitate smooth transitions between action areas.

theory_units.title: Tracking Camera for Increased Visual Combinations
theory_units.summary: Tracking the camera forward or backward with a moving player expands the range of possible visual compositions within a shot, allowing for dynamic framing and interaction.
theory_units.applies_when: When dynamic interaction between moving and stationary players is desired, or to emphasize a player's approach or recession within the frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increases visual interest and flexibility, enables emphasis on specific characters or interactions, and precisely controls the audience's perspective and emotional connection.

theory_units.title: Selective Camera Movement for Emphasis
theory_units.summary: Camera movement doesn't need to span the entire shot; it can be introduced for only a section to highlight specific moments, actions, or changes in composition.
theory_units.applies_when: When a particular part of a shot requires increased attention, dramatic emphasis, or a subtle shift in focus without resorting to a cut.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws the audience's eye to a specific detail or action, intensifies a moment, or subtly shifts the scene's focus and emotional weight.

theory_units.title: Lateral Tracking to Exclude Stationary Subjects
theory_units.summary: A camera tracking laterally can deliberately move to one side, effectively removing a stationary subject from the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wishes to remove a stationary element from the frame, either to simplify the composition, shift focus entirely to a moving subject, or imply separation.
theory_units.expected_effect: Redirection of audience attention to the moving subject, simplification of the frame, or creation of a sense of separation or abandonment for the excluded subject.

theory_units.title: Tracking to Pinpoint Individuals in a Stationary Group
theory_units.summary: When working with a stationary group, a tracking camera can selectively highlight individual members by moving closer to or further from them.
theory_units.applies_when: When the director wants to draw attention to specific individuals within a static group, conveying their importance, emotional reaction, or isolating them for a moment.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates individual emphasis, draws attention to reactions or specific characters, or suggests a character's isolation within a group context.

theory_units.title: Body Position and Dramatic Dominance
theory_units.summary: A performer's body position relative to the camera (open, neutral, closed) directly influences their dramatic strength and perceived dominance within the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When conveying a character's power, vulnerability, assertiveness, or mystery through their physical presence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Open (frontal) positions communicate strength, confidence, and dominance; closed (rear) positions imply weakness, vulnerability, or mystery; and neutral (side) positions offer a balanced, objective view.
theory_units.caution: The dramatic effect of body position is subordinate to context; a closed position can generate interest by keeping identity unknown.

theory_units.title: Integrating Body Position Changes with Walking
theory_units.summary: Changes in a performer's body attitude are more impactful and natural when seamlessly combined with movement, such as walking, making audience manipulation less noticeable.
theory_units.applies_when: When a character's dramatic attitude or focus needs to shift, and the director wants to achieve this subtly and realistically without abrupt changes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Preserves naturalness and realism, prevents the audience from perceiving conscious manipulation, and enhances the emotional or dramatic effectiveness of the attitude change.

theory_units.title: Reversing Actor Positions via In-Depth Movement (Static Camera)
theory_units.summary: A stationary camera can achieve a visual reversal of actor positions by having both players move in depth, with the dominant player moving first.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director wants to change the spatial relationship and perceived dominance between two actors within a single shot without resorting to a cut, creating a 'reverse coverage' effect.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates dynamic compositional changes, maintains continuity within a single shot, and subtly shifts dramatic focus by altering foreground/background relationships.

theory_units.title: Combining Vertical Movement Levels
theory_units.summary: Characters changing vertical levels (e.g., standing to kneeling) can be combined with other characters' levels to create visually dynamic and pleasant vertical compositions.
theory_units.applies_when: When designing interactions between multiple characters to add visual interest, emphasize power dynamics, or create varied compositional lines within the frame.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates visually pleasant and dynamic compositions, reinforces character relationships or power structures through physical levels, and adds depth to the scene.

theory_units.title: Substitution by Sectors (Fixed Camera)
theory_units.summary: A fixed camera is used to substitute one actor with another in a particular screen sector (vertical or depth plane) without moving other actors already present.
theory_units.applies_when: When aiming to change the cast, character focus, or dynamic within a fixed frame, often to maintain a long single shot and avoid cuts, while introducing new characters or changing interactions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains visual continuity and flow within a single shot, introduces or removes characters dynamically, and allows for complex character interactions in a constrained frame while managing audience attention.
theory_units.caution: Requires precise actor blocking and timing to be effective and seamless.

theory_units.title: Three-Sector Composition for Leader and Subordinates
theory_units.summary: Dividing the screen into three vertical sectors, with a leader centrally framed and subordinates entering/exiting from the sides, is ideal for portraying command structures.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting a leader interacting with multiple subordinates, emphasizing the leader's central authority and the interchangeability or succession of followers.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visually reinforces the leader's central role and authority, while subordinates appear to cycle through their positions, serving the leader, creating a clear power hierarchy.

theory_units.title: Dynamic Sector Switching for Variation and Emphasis
theory_units.summary: To avoid monotony in long shots and widen expressive possibilities, actor and camera movement can be used to switch screen sectors, shifting focus and changing compositions.
theory_units.applies_when: When a scene needs to maintain audience engagement over a long shot, requiring dynamic shifts in focus and composition without cuts, or to emphasize specific interactions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents visual monotony, emphasizes important moments or dialogue, and provides varied visual interest, keeping the audience engaged with the evolving scene.

theory_units.title: Upstaging for Dominance during Sector Exchange
theory_units.summary: When players cross over to exchange sectors, the dominant player should be placed slightly 'upstage' (closer to the camera's perspective) and ideally pass in front of the other.
theory_units.applies_when: When two actors exchange positions or cross paths, and one needs to maintain or assert dominance and command audience attention.
theory_units.expected_effect: The dominant player retains audience focus and appears more powerful or central; passing in front actively directs and maintains the audience's attention on the dominant figure.
theory_units.caution: Passing behind the other player can unintentionally shift audience focus to the stationary player, diminishing the dominant player's impact.

theory_units.title: Modifying Dominance with Body Position in Cross-Overs
theory_units.summary: The perceived dominance during an upstage cross-over can be further altered by opening or closing the dominant player's body position relative to the camera.
theory_units.applies_when: When fine-tuning the balance of power or emphasis between characters during movement or interaction, adding subtle layers to their relationship.
theory_units.expected_effect: An open body position enhances the perception of dominance and confidence; a closed position can soften it, suggest vulnerability, or add complexity (e.g., reluctance or internal conflict).

theory_units.title: Emphasizing a Player by Following Their Exit
theory_units.summary: If a player moves out of shot and the camera follows them, that player is emphasized, even if they were not the initially dominant party, making their departure significant.
theory_units.applies_when: When a director wants to draw particular attention to a character leaving the frame, suggesting their importance, the ongoing relevance of their action, or their emotional state.
theory_units.expected_effect: Shifts the audience's focus and importance to the exiting character, making their departure a significant moment rather than a simple disappearance, and can imply continued narrative relevance.

theory_units.title: Compensatory Movement for Stage Balance
theory_units.summary: An actor who has been crossed by another performer moves a short distance in the opposite direction to re-establish visual balance within the frame.
theory_units.applies_when: When an actor crosses another, particularly with a stationary camera, to maintain a balanced composition.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains visual equilibrium on screen and ensures a smooth 'area transposition' of actors.
theory_units.caution: This is an 'old stage convention'; modern filmmaking often uses camera movement as an alternative, especially in close shots.

theory_units.title: Body Position for Dominance and Attention
theory_units.summary: A character's body position (open or closed, upstage or downstage) can modify their perceived dominance, direct audience attention, and contribute to screen composition.
theory_units.applies_when: Staging actors in relation to each other, the camera, or the audience to control focus and power dynamics.
theory_units.expected_effect: Emphasizes specific characters, directs the audience's gaze, and clarifies character relationships or internal states.

theory_units.title: Shifting Audience Attention (Circle 'Dress' Movement)
theory_units.summary: A variant of compensatory movement where an actor performs a half-circle, drawing audience eyes, then uses body position and gaze to shift attention to another actor, and finally another actor re-engages the audience.
theory_units.applies_when: The director wants to fluidly shift audience focus between multiple performers within a continuous shot, without cuts.
theory_units.expected_effect: Actively guides audience gaze between characters, creating a dynamic visual flow and highlighting different points of interest sequentially.
theory_units.caution: Requires precise coordination of actor movements and body language to be effective.

theory_units.title: Motivation for Actor Movement
theory_units.summary: All actor movement on screen, whether on a stage or for a camera, must be clearly motivated or be made to appear so.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning any blocking or movement for characters within a scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances realism and believability of character actions, supports the narrative, and prevents audience distraction or confusion.
theory_units.caution: Unmotivated movement can pull the audience out of the story and make character actions seem arbitrary.

theory_units.title: Panning with Moving Player
theory_units.summary: Instead of actors performing compensatory movements, the camera can pan to follow a moving player, maintaining focus and smoothly re-establishing screen balance.
theory_units.applies_when: An actor moves across the frame, especially when the camera is close or when an actor moves in depth, to keep them in focus and balance the composition.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a smooth, fluid shot that maintains audience focus on the moving subject and avoids jarring compositional shifts or the need for other actors to adjust.

theory_units.title: Tracking Camera for Zone/Sector Change
theory_units.summary: A tracking camera follows moving actors, causing them to exchange screen sectors and change zones dynamically within the frame, creating new compositions.
theory_units.applies_when: The director wants to show actors moving through different spaces or 'zones' while maintaining a continuous shot and creating evolving or new static compositions at the start and end of the track.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enables a fluid and dynamic shot where actors can shift their screen positions and spatial zones smoothly, providing rich visual variations without cuts.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful planning of actor movement and camera path to avoid collisions or lost focus.

theory_units.title: Numerical Contrast
theory_units.summary: The dramatic juxtaposition of one person against a group, or a small group against a larger one, emphasizes characters through isolation or highlights power dynamics.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to highlight an individual's isolation, vulnerability, or power within a group context, or to visually represent changing group dynamics.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates dramatic tension, emphasizes specific characters by isolating them or showing their relationship to a group, and communicates power imbalances visually.
theory_units.caution: Overuse can become predictable; needs to be motivated by the scene's dramatic needs.

theory_units.title: Editing in the Camera Technique
theory_units.summary: A filmmaking approach where scenes are shot only in a single version, without alternative cover shots, requiring precise pre-planning and in-camera decision-making.
theory_units.applies_when: When rapid production is needed and the director has a clear, unyielding vision for each shot, accepting less room for post-production changes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Faster shooting rate; demands a higher degree of initial planning and on-set precision. Limits post-production flexibility.
theory_units.caution: Significantly less room for error during shooting; no alternative coverage to fall back on if the main shot doesn out as planned.

theory_units.title: Shot Size for Simple Dialogue in Limited Space
theory_units.summary: For dialogue scenes where actors move in a limited stage space, use medium or close shot set-ups to maintain focus.
theory_units.applies_when: Covering simple dialogue between actors whose physical movement is restricted to a small area.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains audience focus on dialogue and character expressions, optimizing the limited physical context.

theory_units.title: Employing Geometric Movement Patterns
theory_units.summary: Utilize definite geometrical patterns, particularly circular and triangular paths, for actor blocking and camera movement within a scene.
theory_units.applies_when: Designing actor movement for visual interest and dynamic composition, especially around static elements or other performers in a scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Adds visual dynamism, guides audience attention, and can create complex yet organized compositions that enhance the scene's visual flow.
theory_units.caution: Movement patterns should not feel forced or artificial; they must integrate naturally into the scene's action and dialogue.

theory_units.title: Motivated Actor Movement
theory_units.summary: All actor movement within a scene must appear motivated, ideally by emotion, secondarily by dialogue, or lastly by practical reasons.
theory_units.applies_when: Choreographing any actor movement or staging within a scene.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances realism and audience engagement by making movements feel natural, purposeful, and psychologically grounded, rather than arbitrary.
theory_units.caution: Unmotivated or poorly motivated movement can distract the audience and pull them out of the scene, diminishing believability.

theory_units.title: Zone Change for Dialogue Scene Variation
theory_units.summary: Moving players between distinct areas (zones) of the set introduces visual variety, provides different backgrounds, and allows for changes in physical editing patterns, making static dialogue scenes more dynamic and natural.
theory_units.applies_when: Handling potentially static dialogue scenes to prevent visual stagnation and enhance audience engagement.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased realism, sustained visual interest, and effective masking of repeated editing formulas, making the scene feel more spontaneous.
theory_units.caution: Movement must always be motivated; otherwise, zone changes can feel artificial or forced.

theory_units.title: Zone Change for Emotional and Mood Progression
theory_units.summary: Beyond visual variety, changing zones allows a scene to progress to different levels of emotion and mood, for example, becoming more intimate or tense as the physical space alters.
theory_units.applies_when: Structuring a scene's emotional arc or shifting its tone and character relationships.
theory_units.expected_effect: Subtle yet powerful shifts in the audience's perception of character relationships and the overall scene atmosphere.

theory_units.title: Timing Zone Changes with Re-establishing Shots
theory_units.summary: A change of zone should take place during a re-establishing shot, which serves to bridge two different editing patterns and re-orient the audience to the new spatial arrangement.
theory_units.applies_when: Implementing a zone change within a sequence to ensure smooth and clear transitions.
theory_units.expected_effect: Smooth transitions for the audience, maintaining spatial awareness and clear comprehension of character positions and relationships as they move between areas.

theory_units.title: Varying Composition and Mood in Zone Changes
theory_units.summary: Even if editing patterns repeat across different zones, varying actor screen positions, body levels (e.g., sitting down), and distances significantly alters pictorial composition and can enhance intimacy or other emotional states.
theory_units.applies_when: Designing the specifics of actor placement, posture, and proxemics within different zones.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates fresh visual compositions and emotional shifts, preventing repetition from feeling stale and deepening character relationships or scene dynamics.

theory_units.title: Strategic Number of Zones for Staging
theory_units.summary: Typically, three to five distinct areas (zones) on a set are sufficient for staging a sequence, as each area can be effectively reused to maintain variety.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning the physical layout and blocking for a scene that involves zone changes or complex actor movements.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides ample visual variation without overcomplicating the set design or blocking, allowing for strategic reuse of areas.
theory_units.caution: Too many zones might become confusing for the audience or complicate production; too few might limit the desired visual variety.

theory_units.title: Creating the Illusion of Spontaneity
theory_units.summary: Consciously plan subtle variations in attitudes, body positions, and distances between actors to achieve an illusion of natural spontaneity, even when using predefined formulas or patterns.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing actor interactions and blocking within any scene, particularly those involving established formulas.
theory_units.expected_effect: Makes the scene feel more authentic and less 'staged' for the audience, enhancing immersion and believability.

theory_units.title: Group Expansion Techniques
theory_units.summary: Achieve visual group expansion either through selective editing to highlight individuals on the periphery or by physically moving some figures from the central group to another area.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to broaden the focus of a group scene, introduce new visual elements, or subtly shift attention within a group.
theory_units.expected_effect: Varies pictorial composition, can emphasize individual characters within a group context, and visually opens up the scene.
theory_units.caution: Ensure the expansion feels motivated by the narrative or character dynamics, and not merely for visual effect.

theory_units.title: Emphasizing Silent Players with Selective Editing
theory_units.summary: Use selective editing, such as cutting to a silent player on the rim of a group, to emphasize their presence, reactions, or to achieve pictorial variation.
theory_units.applies_when: When there's a silent observer or a character whose unspoken reaction or presence is important to the scene's meaning.
theory_units.expected_effect: Draws audience attention to a specific character's unspoken role or internal state, adding depth and nuance to the scene without dialogue.

theory_units.title: Group Expansion through Individual Movement
theory_units.summary: When one player moves from an initial zone to a second while their companion remains in the first, it effectively creates a visual expansion of the group and alters spatial relationships.
theory_units.applies_when: When needing to expand a two-person or small group scene visually without moving everyone, or to highlight a character's emotional or physical journey.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates visual interest, subtly alters the perceived spatial and emotional relationship between characters, and can emphasize the moving character's independence or purpose.

theory_units.title: Combining Techniques for Long Sequences
theory_units.summary: For extended sequences, combine group zone changes with individual player movement and group expansion to add continuous visual variety and maintain audience engagement.
theory_units.applies_when: Designing and staging extended dialogue or character interaction sequences that require sustained visual interest.
theory_units.expected_effect: Prevents visual monotony and maintains audience engagement over longer periods, making complex scenes feel dynamic and unforced.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful and meticulous planning to ensure smooth transitions and clear motivations for all movements and compositional shifts.

theory_units.title: Camera Movement with Moving Actor
theory_units.summary: The camera can actively pan or track (forward/backward) with a moving actor, especially when that player is moving alone between zones.
theory_units.applies_when: Following a single actor's movement across a set, between distinct zones, or emphasizing their journey.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains focus on the moving character, reinforces their journey or purpose, and can emphasize their isolation or determination within the space.

theory_units.title: Justifying Movement with 'Bits of Business'
theory_units.summary: Incorporate small, practical actions, known as 'bits of business' (e.g., lighting a cigarette, moving a prop), into an actor's movement to naturally justify their zone changes or movement across the set.
theory_units.applies_when: When an actor needs to move, but there isn't a strong emotional or dialogue-based motivation, or to add subtle realism.
theory_units.expected_effect: Makes the actor's movement appear more natural and integrated into the scene's reality, preventing it from feeling arbitrary or unmotivated.
theory_units.caution: 'Bits of business' should be subtle and should not distract from the main action, dialogue, or character emotion of the scene.

theory_units.title: Group Contraction for Sequence Conclusion
theory_units.summary: Reuniting scattered players in a single area to effectively conclude a scene or sequence, often after a period of expansion.
theory_units.applies_when: Concluding a sequence where characters have been expanded or scattered across zones and a sense of resolution is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides a sense of resolution and finality to the scene, visually bringing characters together.

theory_units.title: Story-Driven Movement Patterns (Expand/Contract)
theory_units.summary: Ensure that patterns of character movement, such as group expansion and contraction, are motivated by the story and not arbitrarily imposed.
theory_units.applies_when: Planning character blocking and movement patterns, especially those involving group expansion or contraction across different zones.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances narrative coherence and avoids distracting the audience with unmotivated movement, serving the story's emotional or thematic needs.
theory_units.caution: Avoid arbitrary imposition of movement patterns; prioritize the most adequate editing solution that supports the narrative.

theory_units.title: Clarifying Zone Changes with Re-establishing Shots
theory_units.summary: Effect changes of zone during the introduction of a re-establishing shot to clearly show the two zones involved and underline the geography of the situation.
theory_units.applies_when: Whenever characters transition between distinct physical zones within a scene, particularly if the audience needs to understand the new spatial relationships.
theory_units.expected_effect: Maintains the audience's understanding of spatial relationships and scene geography, preventing confusion about character locations.

theory_units.title: Enhancing Depth in Long Pan Shots
theory_units.summary: Incorporate static objects or props in the foreground during long pan shots to add depth to the camera's movement and the overall composition.
theory_units.applies_when: Executing long pan shots, especially when following moving subjects or revealing a new environment, and a stronger sense of three-dimensionality is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a stronger sense of three-dimensionality and visual interest within the frame, making the movement feel more dynamic and immersive.

theory_units.title: Delayed Zone Change for Natural Flow
theory_units.summary: Delay the zone change of a second player by introducing an interplay of shots to create a smoother, less artificial transition between zones.
theory_units.applies_when: Moving multiple players smoothly between zones, particularly when a direct, simultaneous or immediate transition might feel abrupt or artificial.
theory_units.expected_effect: Enhances the natural flow of action and character movement, making transitions feel more organic and visually pleasing.
theory_units.caution: Introduce only whenever the situation warrants it to move players smoothly from zone to zone.

theory_units.title: Shot-by-Shot Dialogue Editing
theory_units.summary: A technique for dialogue scenes where the scene is covered in as many individual shots as necessary, with each shot often dedicated to a single phrase or group of lines, and frequently avoiding re-using camera sites or parallel editing between shots.
theory_units.applies_when: Directing dialogue sequences where precise control over each line's visual presentation is desired, or in scenes of pure action where performers move without depending on dialogue.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a highly deliberate and often sequential narrative flow, emphasizing each spoken segment and visual change, providing pictorial variety.
theory_units.caution: Requires a solid knowledge of film technique, as an accumulation of errors while shooting will offer less opportunity for correction in post-production. Examples often use each shot only once and avoid parallel splicing.

theory_units.title: Flexibility of Parallel Editing
theory_units.summary: Parallel editing allows filmmakers to easily adjust the timing and duration of shots for different lines of action because each action is visually independent.
theory_units.applies_when: When depicting multiple, simultaneous, or alternating lines of action, or when greater control over post-production timing is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increased control over sequence tempo (to increase or slacken); easier modification and adjustment of shot duration during editing.
theory_units.caution: Continuous shot-by-shot editing offers less control over modifications once material is shot and printed.

theory_units.title: Single Shots as Visual Statements
theory_units.summary: Employing single shots to present individual facts or ideas, making each shot equivalent to a phrase or short statement, capable of conveying ideas without spoken words.
theory_units.applies_when: When presenting information clearly and concisely without dialogue, or when building a sequence with distinct visual points.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clear and concise communication of facts or ideas; reliance on images to convey narrative; deliberate control over the rhythm of information delivery.

theory_units.title: Reaction Shots for Commentary
theory_units.summary: Intercutting silent or live sound reaction shots into a master shot to comment on events or performers not currently visible in the master shot, or to stress specific elements.
theory_units.applies_when: Whenever necessary to show a character's response, add visual commentary, or emphasize a specific action, dialogue, or element within a master shot.
theory_units.expected_effect: Provides audience with additional information or emotional context; stresses action, dialogue, or elements; covers off-screen events or reactions.
theory_units.caution: Should be intercut 'whenever necessary', implying not to overuse them.

theory_units.title: Technique Serves the Scene (Guiding Principle)
theory_units.summary: All filmmaking techniques must primarily serve the scene's intention, aiming for natural and lifelike visual results, rather than technique dictating the scene itself.
theory_units.applies_when: Throughout all stages of filmmaking, especially when choosing and applying specific techniques or evaluating their effectiveness.
theory_units.expected_effect: Authentic and natural-looking visuals that effectively convey the filmmaker's intentions and the nuances of acting performance.
theory_units.caution: Technique defeats its purpose if it fails to convey the filmmaker's intentions and the subtleties of acting performed.

theory_units.title: Fade-out/Fade-in for Time Transitions
theory_units.summary: A laboratory-effect transition where the screen image gradually darkens (fade out) and is replaced by another image which gradually lightens (fade in), used to signify the passage of time.
theory_units.applies_when: Moving between sequences across a significant passage of time.
theory_units.expected_effect: A clear, soft, and gradual indication of time passing; a smooth transition between scenes.
theory_units.caution: If insufficient film footage is available, the last frame of the scene can be 'frozen' before fading out or in.

theory_units.title: Color Fades for Mood and Relationship
theory_units.summary: Using fades to or from a dominant color (or combination of colors) to indicate time passage and subtly suggest a mood or thematic relationship between connected sequences.
theory_units.applies_when: Transitioning between scenes when wishing to visually emphasize or suggest a specific emotional tone or thematic connection.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visual punctuation of time passage; establishment or reinforcement of mood; subtle suggestion of relationships between sequences.
theory_units.caution: None explicitly stated, but implies thoughtful choice of colors to align with the desired mood.

theory_units.title: Dissolve for Scene Transitions
theory_units.summary: A combination of a fade out and a fade in, superimposed on the same strip of film, providing a transition between scenes.
theory_units.applies_when: Moving between scenes, indicating the passage of time, or relating the mood of two scenes.
theory_units.expected_effect: A smooth, blended transition; can indicate time passage; can relate the moods of two scenes.
theory_units.caution: When used for apparition effects, the camera cannot be moved during the stationary parts of the scene to retain even intensity.

theory_units.title: Wipe for Scene Transitions
theory_units.summary: A laboratory effect where a new scene is introduced by pushing or wiping the first scene off the screen, or by a travelling line erasing the old scene to reveal the new.
theory_units.applies_when: Introducing a new scene, particularly for time transitions, or when a distinct, graphic transition is desired.
theory_units.expected_effect: A distinct and often graphic transition between scenes.
theory_units.caution: More complicated or startling wipe patterns (e.g., spiraling wipes) are generally reserved for film trailers due to their intense effect and potential for distraction.

theory_units.title: Iris Effect for Attention/Closure
theory_units.summary: A diminishing or expanding circle that originally centered attention on an isolated subject or detail, often used as a closing effect.
theory_units.applies_when: Centering audience attention on a specific detail, or as a stylized closing/opening effect for a sequence.
theory_units.expected_effect: Focuses audience attention; provides a clear, often stylized, closure or opening.
theory_units.caution: Was abandoned as a time transition method due to overuse; can become cliché if not creatively revived.

theory_units.title: Using Dark Areas for Transitions
theory_units.summary: Transitioning between scenes by panning or tracking the camera behind a dark area or shape that temporarily fills the screen, then cutting to a similar opening device in the next scene.
theory_units.applies_when: Creating a smooth, often hidden, transition between scenes, especially when location or time changes.
theory_units.expected_effect: Smoother transition that can mask the cut; a momentary distraction that guides the audience from one scene to the next.
theory_units.caution: Transition will be smoother if the camera moves in the same direction in both shots, rather than opposed.

theory_units.title: Titles for Sequence Separation and Information
theory_units.summary: Using titles to clearly identify places, specific times of day, or years, appearing over relevant imagery or plain backgrounds.
theory_units.applies_when: Introducing new sequences, establishing setting (time or place), or providing concise narrative information.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clear and concise communication of setting or temporal information; efficient narrative exposition.

theory_units.title: Time Props for Passage of Time
theory_units.summary: Employing specific props that visibly change or are consumed over a short period to symbolize the passage of time, often using dissolves to show the transformation.
theory_units.applies_when: Visually depicting the passage of time without explicit dates or long, drawn-out sequences, relying on symbolic visual cues.
theory_units.expected_effect: Clear, symbolic representation of time's passing; a subtle visual cue for temporal shifts.
theory_units.caution: Many traditional time props (e.g., lighted candles, cigarettes, clocks, calendars) are now cliches and should be used mindfully.

theory_units.title: Light Change for Time Transitions
theory_units.summary: Altering studio lighting on a motionless set to simulate the gradual change from morning to evening, thereby indicating a time transition.
theory_units.applies_when: Depicting a significant passage of time within the same location without a cut or major scene change.
theory_units.expected_effect: A gradual, natural-looking shift in lighting and shadows that clearly signifies the passage of time.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful control of studio lights to achieve a believable, gradual effect.

theory_units.title: Question and Answer for Transition
theory_units.summary: Using dialogue where a question posed by a character in one scene is answered by a different character in a new location and time, with the spoken words forming the transition link.
theory_units.applies_when: Creating a thematic or narrative link between disparate scenes or locations based on spoken dialogue.
theory_units.expected_effect: An intellectual or narrative transition based on the continuity of ideas, rather than visuals, connecting different contexts through speech.
theory_units.caution: The questioner and the person answering should not be related by the direction of their looks to emphasize the distinct scene separation.

theory_units.title: Movement in the Same Direction for Transition
theory_units.summary: Transitioning between scenes by having a vehicle or character exit one shot moving in a specific direction, and then enter the next shot moving in the same direction, even if the location, time, and mood have changed.
theory_units.applies_when: Creating a fluid, visually continuous transition between disparate settings, times, or moods.
theory_units.expected_effect: A smooth visual flow despite changes in setting; creates a subconscious link for the audience.
theory_units.caution: Requires precise planning to ensure consistent direction of movement across the cut.

theory_units.title: Substitution of an Object for Transition
theory_units.summary: Linking sequences through a sudden cut between two shots where an object or its effect in the first shot is visually or thematically substituted by a similar object or effect in the second, often tied by a similar sound.
theory_units.applies_when: Creating a surprising, symbolic, or abrupt transition between seemingly unrelated scenes, using a strong visual or sonic link.
theory_units.expected_effect: A strong, often jarring or symbolic, connection between two scenes; creates visual or sonic surprise.
theory_units.caution: The link must be clearly provided by a similar sound or effect to be effective.

theory_units.title: Word Repetition for Transition
theory_units.summary: Ending one sequence with a character speaking a specific word in close shot and beginning the next with a new player repeating that same word in a different place, time, or context.
theory_units.applies_when: Creating an auditory or thematic link between two otherwise separate scenes, using dialogue as the bridge.
theory_units.expected_effect: Establishes a narrative or thematic connection through sound; can change emphasis for new meaning as the new scene develops.

theory_units.title: Deceptive Visual Match for Transition
theory_units.summary: Creating a scene transition by relying on an element at the end of one shot and the beginning of the next, where that element initially suggests continuity but then reveals a significant change in scene, time, or location.
theory_units.applies_when: Bridging a period of time or change in location while initially creating a strong sense of seamless visual continuity to then reveal a new context.
theory_units.expected_effect: The viewer initially perceives continuity, then realizes a new sequence has begun, providing a subtle or surprising transition.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful planning of the 'matching' element to ensure the initial deception and subsequent reveal are effective.

theory_units.title: Abstract to Concrete for Transition
theory_units.summary: Beginning a scene transition with an abstract visual element that is initially unidentifiable, then revealing its meaning and context through the introduction of a human reference or other clarifying element.
theory_units.applies_when: Creating a visually intriguing, disorienting, or symbolic transition that gradually reveals its context.
theory_units.expected_effect: Visual surprise; forces the audience to re-evaluate the image; creates a unique and thought-provoking scene opening.
theory_units.caution: Requires a clear and timely 'reveal' to ensure the abstract image acquires meaning for the audience.

theory_units.title: Visual Shock for Flashy Transitions
theory_units.summary: Employing a visually jarring or surprising element to create a 'flashy' scene transition, often involving an object or person suddenly blocking or replacing the image.
theory_units.applies_when: Desiring a strong, attention-grabbing, or disorienting transition, particularly for a 'flashy' scene or a dramatic shift.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates significant visual impact and surprise; a sudden shift in audience perception or setting.
theory_units.caution: Visual shock should be increased or used judiciously to avoid over-the-top or unmotivated effects.

theory_units.title: Camera Movement Alone for Transition
theory_units.summary: Using camera movement by itself to effect a scene transition, relying on an initial close shot or close-up to momentarily distract the audience before the movement reveals the true context of the new shot.
theory_units.applies_when: Creating a dynamic transition that uses camera motion to unveil a new scene, place, or time, often masking the cut through initial tight framing.
theory_units.expected_effect: A fluid and surprising reveal of the new scene; a smooth transition that masks the cut through initial distraction.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful framing of the initial close shot to provide sufficient distraction before the camera movement reveals the new context.

theory_units.title: Deceptive Visual Match for Time Transition
theory_units.summary: Create a time gap between two shots that appear to have a continuous visual axis, then reveal the elapsed time with camera movement or a close shot masking the surroundings.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to omit uninteresting or lengthy time lapses within a scene or between scenes, while maintaining a sense of smooth visual flow initially.
theory_units.expected_effect: Audience experiences a subtle surprise or realization of a time jump, making the transition feel quick and efficient without an explicit dissolve or fade.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful planning of visual elements to create the initial deception and subsequent revelation.

theory_units.title: Character Close-Up as Inter-Scene Bridge
theory_units.summary: Employ a close-up of a central character with a neutral background to smoothly transition between two different scenes or time periods where the character appears, allowing a location or time change to be masked.
theory_units.applies_when: A director needs to transition between distinct scenes or locations with the same character, wanting to mask the change subtly and keep focus on the character's emotional state or reaction.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a seamless, almost invisible transition, making the audience connect the character's internal state across different external contexts. The surprise of the new location is delayed and often visually striking.
theory_units.caution: Requires careful selection of background to ensure neutrality and proper pacing of the camera pull-back.

theory_units.title: Prop Close-Up as Inter-Scene Bridge
theory_units.summary: Utilize a close-up of a significant prop to create a time or location transition between scenes, where the prop reappears in a new context in the subsequent scene, masking the change.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to bridge a time or location gap using an object as a visual anchor, making the transition feel quick and purely cinematic.
theory_units.expected_effect: Smoothly connects two disparate scenes through a shared object, allowing for significant shifts in time, place, or even characters to be introduced seamlessly.
theory_units.caution: The prop must be visually distinct and its reappearance in the new context must make narrative sense or contribute to the surprise.

theory_units.title: Unrelated Object Close-Up Scene Transition
theory_units.summary: Transition between scenes by cutting to a sudden close-up of an object or person, which is then revealed in its full context within the new scene, acting as a visual bridge.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to quickly move from one scene to a completely different one, using an object as an initial focal point to establish the new location or theme.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates an abrupt yet visually intriguing transition, drawing the audience's attention to a specific detail before expanding their view to the new environment.
theory_units.caution: The object chosen should either foreshadow the new scene's content or provide a visually engaging mystery that is resolved in the subsequent shot.

theory_units.title: Parallel Editing for Flashback/Flashforward
theory_units.summary: Introduce a time shift (flashback or flashforward) by intercutting close-ups of a character's reaction or a visual cue with the source of that cue, then revealing the new time/location through a camera movement.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to smoothly and visually introduce a non-linear narrative element (flashback/forward) using a visual motif or character focus as the bridge.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a visually fluent and often surprising transition into a different time, linking the present moment to the past or future through a common visual thread. Rapid cutting can heighten intensity.
theory_units.caution: The visual cue must be strong enough to carry the parallel, and the revelation must be clear. Overuse of rapid cutting can feel self-conscious.

theory_units.title: Neutral Scene Openers
theory_units.summary: Begin a scene neutrally, either by moving an actor or the camera, to gradually introduce the main event or character and avoid abrupt emphasis.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to introduce a new scene or event without immediately throwing undue emphasis on it, allowing the audience to gradually enter the new context.
theory_units.expected_effect: Creates a smoother, less abrupt entry into a new scene, guiding the audience's attention and pacing the reveal of crucial information.

theory_units.title: Subjective Point of View Introduction
theory_units.summary: Convey a character's subjective point of view by showing them in a close shot, then cutting to a shot taken from their eye-line (excluding them), which can be emphasized by movement and direct gaze at the camera.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants the audience to experience the scene directly through a character's eyes, emphasizing their perspective, emotions, or what they are focusing on.
theory_units.expected_effect: Increases audience identification with the character, creates immersion, and can heighten suspense or emotional impact, especially when combined with camera movement or direct address (gaze into camera).
theory_units.caution: Can be disorienting if overused or not clearly established.

theory_units.title: Interrupted Subjective POV for Impact
theory_units.summary: Break a subjective tracking shot with a static, objective shot to re-establish the subject and emphasize by contrast the subjective experience.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to intensify the impact of a subjective experience (e.g., a car hurtling towards a crash) by briefly pulling out to an objective view, then returning.
theory_units.expected_effect: The static, objective shot re-establishes context and, by its lack of camera action, highlights the frantic or intense nature of the preceding/following subjective view, enhancing the dramatic impact.
theory_units.caution: The interruption should be brief and strategically placed to maximize contrast and avoid breaking immersion too much.

theory_units.title: Unidentified Subjective POV Cues
theory_units.summary: Introduce a subjective point of view without first identifying the observer, using visual cues like binocular shapes, gunsights, dominant color filters, or foreground movement combined with off-screen hushed voices.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to create immediate suspense, mystery, or a sense of an unseen observer, before or without explicitly revealing who is seeing.
theory_units.expected_effect: Engages the audience's curiosity, places them directly into an unknown observer's shoes, and can create a sense of unease, surveillance, or an impending event.
theory_units.caution: The cues must be strong enough for the audience to implicitly understand it's a POV shot, even without an identified observer.

theory_units.title: Jump Cuts for Punctuation
theory_units.summary: Employ abrupt, visible jump cuts between shots of a static or slowly moving subject, often on a common visual axis, to punctuate a moment, stress a revelation, or introduce new elements with emphasis.
theory_units.applies_when: A director wants to create a jarring effect, draw strong attention to a detail, build tension, or provide a dramatic reveal by intentionally breaking visual continuity.
theory_units.expected_effect: Delivers a sudden jolt to the audience, heightens emotional impact (e.g., shock, surprise), directs focus, and can make mundane objects or moments feel more significant.
theory_units.caution: Can look self-conscious or amateurish if not used judiciously and with clear artistic intent. 'Sound judgment must be employed.'

theory_units.title: Jump Cuts for Time Compression
theory_units.summary: Utilize jump cuts to eliminate uninteresting segments of time within a scene or between scenes, conveying the passage of time or a progression of actions efficiently.
theory_units.applies_when: A director needs to condense a repetitive, mundane, or lengthy activity into a short sequence, showing progression or elapsed time without explicitly revealing the cuts.
